articles.title: Sally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action support
articles.summary:
Irish writer of Normal People says she can no longer receive royalties from British sales and she cancelled UK trip due to fear of arrest

Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to…

blocks.text: Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.
The Irish novelist, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, said her public support for the direct action group meant she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.

After Palestine Action was banned last year, Rooney said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Supporting organisations banned under the Terrorism Act is an offence and she subsequently cancelled a trip to the UK to pick up an award, for fear of arrest.

In a statement provided to the Guardian, the bestselling author said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.

“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”

In a high court statement in support of the legal challenge to proscription, warning against its impact on freedom of expression, Rooney said her books could disappear from UK stores and the publication of new works in the UK could be prevented.

Her books have been critically acclaimed – she has been described as the voice of a generation – and hugely commercially successful in the UK. Normal People has sold more than 1m copies, while Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000. Normal People and Conversations With Friends were also adapted by the BBC, with the former racking up 62.7m views and becoming the broadcaster’s most-streamed series of 2020.

Rooney said last year that she had been advised by the independent producer of the TV dramatisations that any payment to her for those series, both broadcast before the ban, would be a breach of terrorism laws if it knew or suspected that she was using the royalties to fund Palestine Action.

Section 15 of the Terrorism Act makes it an offence if a person “provides money or other property, and knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism”. It carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.

Her UK and Ireland publisher, Faber said: “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.

“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”

More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned in July last year, most for holding placards saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”

About 2,500 people have been charged, although none have been tried as a legal challenge to the ban is continuing and will be heard by the supreme court next month. Most arrests and charges have related to section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum jail term of six months.

articles.title: Uber begins self-driving robotaxi trial in Manchester
articles.summary:
Company hails first step in rolling out technology across UK as first autonomous vehicles take to city’s streets

Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as…

blocks.text: Uber has begun a trial of autonomous vehicles on the streets of Manchester as it looks to bring robotaxis to cities around the UK.

The first self-driving cars are operating, using the technology of its partner firms Pony and Verne, with whom Uber recently launched Europe’s first autonomous taxi service in the Croatian capital, Zagreb.
Uber said it was “excited to take this first step toward making this technology accessible to people across the UK”.
In social media posts, Verne said it had “started our autonomous vehicle testing in Manchester”, while Pony said there were “plans to bring robotaxis to the city” and that testing was under way.
The tests involve the company mapping the streets of the city in north-west England with a safety driver behind the wheel and no passengers.
Limited passenger services started last month in London, but with a safety driver in the front seat of cars supplied by Wayve under Transport for London’s licensing rules for private hire vehicles.

The next steps are unclear. Opposition from Uber drivers, their unions and the capital’s politicians to the rollout of robotaxis is mounting. The GMB and ADCU unions have both said thousands of drivers jobs will be lost and have called for help for those affected.
A critical report from London assembly’s transport committee this week called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services.

It said there was “considerable uncertainty about many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers.

There has been no official application to launch passenger services in Manchester so far, and the vehicles are operating under government licence via the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) and the Department for Transport.
A spokesperson for Transport for Greater Manchester said it wanted the city’s taxis to be the safest in the country.

House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos has bolted the ruling Partido Federal ng Pilipinas to join the Lakas-CMD, sources in the House of Representatives and Lakas told GMA News.
Sandro’s father, President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr., ran for president under the PFP and is now the party’s chairman.

articles.title: ‘A big responsibility’: Clifton Suspension Bridge master hails £7.6m renovation
articles.summary:
Engineer Tristan Ralph describes task of maintaining and running Bristol structure without public money

The job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across…

blocks.text: The job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across the great structure, but the title “bridge master” does have a certain ring to it.

“I don’t tend to say I’m the bridge master when I’m at a party,” said Tristan Ralph, the current holder of the title. “But people do seem to know and bring it up. It’s a job less ordinary, isn’t it? It’s a Victorian sounding title and people are really, really interested.”
There is, however, nothing ceremonial about the title. Ralph is in charge of maintaining and running the Clifton Suspension Bridge, a UK feat of engineering, without any public money.

“It does feel a big responsibility,” said Ralph. “When the chairman of the trustees rang to say we’d like you to do it, you suddenly feel the pressure. It’s so famous and people in Bristol, quite rightly, are proud and almost possessive of it. Bristolians think: ‘It’s our bridge.’”

The bridge master – and the not-for-profit charity the Clifton Suspension Bridge Trust – have the task of maintaining the bridge “in perpetuity”. “I’m a temporary custodian,” Ralph said. “When I’m finished, I have to make sure it is handed on in just [as] good a condition or better than I inherited it.”

blocks.caption: The project took two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing energy-efficient lighting. Photograph: Sam Frost/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ralph, a bridge engineer by profession, was speaking to mark the conclusion of a large refurbishment project that has taken two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing an energy-efficient lighting system. It has cost about £7.5m. “It’s been a big job,” he said. “But it’s come pretty much bang on budget, which is rare these days.”

That is important because, to many visitors’ surprise, the bridge does not receive public funding. “The upkeep of the bridge, the running of it, the salary costs and everything are all paid only by our toll money,” said Ralph. “People think that we might get something from local or central government. But, no, it’s just the toll money.”

Motorised vehicles – including motorcycles – pay £1 to cross the bridge. There is no charge for pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders. As well as being a beautiful structure, it is also a vital part of Bristol and North Somerset’s transport system.

blocks.caption: The refurbishment was the largest in the bridge’s history. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian

blocks.text: Ralph said: “It draws the tourists in. We get visitors from hundreds of countries every year but primarily, it’s still a vital piece of local infrastructure. If the bridge wasn’t here, the difference it would make to Bristol traffic would be incredible. We average over 8,000 vehicles a day still. Maintaining it as a transport link is utterly vital.”
The end of the refurbishment does not mean Ralph can rest on his laurels and spend more time hobnobbing with members of the Bridge Owners Forum.

“In a few years, we’ll need to paint the underside of the bridge. The under-bridge gantry unit itself will be replaced over the coming years. So there’s always something. We need to keep on top of things. It’s like your house or your car. If you just ignore it, don’t do things for a couple of years, they start breaking down.”

blocks.caption: The project came in almost on budget, which is important as the bridge’s upkeep, running and staff costs are all paid using toll money. Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The Guardian

blocks.text: As in most walks of life, the climate emergency is a challenge Ralph and the trust are having to face. “We were monitoring the bridge daily in the summer with the very hot weather. And maybe if the bridge was being designed today, there would be a little bit more robustness around wind.”

The prevailing south-west wind is not usually a problem and the bridge rarely has to close but if it blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be more difficult. “We need to keep an eye at both the magnitude of any wind events but also their frequency,” Ralph said.
The engineer admires the bridge’s designers, including Isambard Kingdom Brunel. “It’s remarkably advanced for its time.”

blocks.caption: The bridge rarely has to close, but if the wind blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be difficult. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA

blocks.text: And there is no sign that its days are numbered, largely because the Victorians did not skimp. Ralph said: “There are three layers of chains. The original Brunel design only had two, but because it went from a timber design to a cast-iron deck, they upped it to three.
“There’s a little bit of comfort in there. Today there might be pressure to say, well, can you keep it to two, but in Victorian times they did like to add a little bit of meat on the bones.

“It doesn’t have a finite life. There’s no end date in our plans. We all just keep it going in the highest standards as we can. It’s in really good condition as long as we keep doing what we need to do, keep our attention on it and don’t let things drift. Forever is a long time but there’s no reason why we have any need to worry at the moment.”

articles.title: New York Public Radio, Rappler co-present ‘Democracy Dialogues’ on October 15, US time
articles.summary: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa joins WNYC’s Brian Lehrer in New York for a live conversation on defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of artificial intelligence

blocks.text: Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa joins WNYC’s Brian Lehrer in New York for a live conversation on defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of artificial intelligence

New York Public Radio (NYPR) and Rappler, the Philippines’ leading digital media company, are proud to co-present the next edition of NYPR’s ongoing live event series “Democracy Dialogues” on Thursday, October 15 at The Greene Space (44 Charlton Street).

The program will feature WNYC’s Brian Lehrer, host of the Peabody Award-winning “The Brian Lehrer Show,” alongside Nobel Laureate Maria Ressa, one of the world’s most prominent advocates for journalism and co-founder and CEO of Rappler. The event will be live streamed on wnyc.org, Rappler.com, C-SPAN and YouTube at 7 pm ET (October 16, 7 am PH time). Portions of the conversation will air on WNYC as part of “The Brian Lehrer Show” on Friday, October 16 at 10 am ET. The full conversation will air as a special on WNYC at a later date.

“Democracy Dialogues” is New York Public Radio’s live event series that examines the state of democracy and the essential roles journalism, free expression and an informed public play in sustaining it. In this conversation, Lehrer and Ressa will focus on understanding, defending and rebuilding democracy in the age of AI.

The event will take place at The Jerome L. Greene Performance Space (“The Greene Space”), NYPR’s street-level event space and broadcast studio in Lower Manhattan, located at 44 Charlton Street. Tickets are available now by visiting https://wnyc.org/events/democracy-dialogues.
About Maria Ressa

Maria Ressa is the co-founder and CEO of Rappler, the Philippines’ independent news organization. Rappler has been a target of the country’s authoritarian government for its investigative reporting on corruption and malfeasance at the hands of the Duterte administration and endured multiple arrests in attempts to silence her, ultimately winning multiple accolades for her reporting and bravery. In addition to the Nobel Peace Prize, she won the UNESCO World Press Freedom Prize in 2021, was TIME’s Person of the Year in 2018, and was also named by TIME as one of the most inspiring and influential women of the century. Ressa is the author of a new book, “The Fight Back: A Citizen’s Guide to Standing Up to Dictators,” available on October 13, 2026.
About New York Public Radio

With an urban vibrancy and a global perspective, New York Public Radio (NYPR) produces innovative, critically acclaimed programming for local and national broadcast, on-demand and live-streaming audiences. NYPR’s brands include WNYC, WQXR, WNYC Studios, Gothamist, New Jersey Public Radio and The Jerome L. Greene Performance Space. The WNYC newsroom and Gothamist produce award-winning local journalism for New York City, New Jersey and the surrounding region. WQXR, the city’s only all-classical radio station, broadcasts new and archival classical recordings and makes live performances from New York City’s esteemed performance venues available to all. WNYC Studios is a premier producer of on-demand and national broadcast audio, and home to some of the industry’s most impactful award-winning podcasts and national radio shows, including “Radiolab,” “On the Media” and “The New Yorker Radio Hour,” among others. The Jerome L. Greene Performance Space is NYPR’s intimate street-level broadcast studio and live event space. Further information about programs, podcasts and stations may be found at www.nypublicradio.org.
About Rappler

Founded in 2012 by Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa and a group of veteran Filipino journalists, Rappler has grown into one of the Philippines’ leading independent news organizations, recognized for its fearless investigative journalism and innovative use of technology. At a time when disinformation and attacks on press freedom threaten democratic institutions, Rappler has remained committed to journalism that holds power to account, exposes corruption and abuses, and delivers meaningful impact in the communities it serves.

Through independent journalism and technology-driven civic engagement, Rappler continues to champion a future where facts matter, communities have a voice, and technology serves democracy rather than undermines it. – Rappler.com

articles.title: French minister accuses Elon Musk of ‘online harassment campaigns’ against European leaders
articles.summary:
Jean-Noël Barrot criticises X owner in speech attacking foreign efforts to destabilise country before 2027 election

France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media…
articles.byline: Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent

blocks.text: France’s foreign minister has accused Elon Musk of using his social media platform to orchestrate “massive online harassment campaigns” against European leaders as he took aim at foreign efforts to destabilise the country before next year’s presidential election.

Speaking at an Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development conference on Tuesday, Jean-Noël Barrot pointed to the role that social media had come to play in the global battle over democracy. “The forces seeking to undermine democracy now dominate the information landscape, where they employ tactics designed to polarise public debate,” he said.
The result was that “political movements with authoritarian aims”, which “play right into the hands of democracy’s declared enemies”, had been gaining ground in Europe and North America, he said.
“They exacerbate the polarisation of our societies,” he added. “Their ultimate goal is clear: to seize power and then create the conditions to never relinquish it.”

Barrot cited the 2027 presidential election in France, where the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner in the polls. “The enemies of democracy are doing everything they can to destabilise us,” he said. “They exploit our divisions and use immigration, secularism and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict to stoke hatred and tensions.”

He listed several other examples, from an unnamed Israeli company accused of creating fake French social media accounts to influence perceptions of the Israel-Gaza war, to accusations that Azerbaijan stirred up tensions amid deadly riots in the French Pacific territory New Caledonia.

Barrot also singled out Musk, the world’s richest man and owner of the social media platform X. “There are massive online harassment campaigns launched by Elon Musk against European leaders in order to influence debates by exploiting the virality of his social media platform.”
Musk did not reply to a request for comment.

Barrot also cited the protests that have rocked France in recent weeks, as schoolchildren, students and trade unionists blockaded schools and marched through cities. The events, said Barrot, had been exploited by “hostile narratives” from Russia, China and Iran, as well as those associated with the Maga movement in the US.

Last week Musk and the US president, Donald Trump, weighed in on the protests in France, seeking to recast them through a lens of mass migration and brushing aside protesters’ demands for better school conditions.
after newsletter promotion

Barrot said his government was working to respond to a reality in which paid or commissioned influencers sought to explore the viral reach of digital platforms. “The Kremlin’s goal is explicitly stated: to put an end to our liberal democracies in favour of a new authoritarianism. Other actors are converging on this goal, seeking to dictate to Europe which democracies are ‘good’ and which are ‘bad’ based on whether they align with their own interests,” he said.
The French minister’s remarks come days after the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was “clear” that Russia had interfered in the Brexit referendum.

Barrot said his government would work to counter these efforts by foreign entities. “We are uncompromising, because it is clear to us that they undermine the nation’s fundamental interests,” he said. “We do not tolerate any foreign interference, from wherever it may come. It is a matter of sovereignty.”

articles.title: US inflation rose to 3.7% in September, figures show
articles.summary:
Final inflation report before midterms comes as polls show widespread anger over cost of living under Trump

Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation…

blocks.text: Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released on Wednesday.

US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7% in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.
Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Consumer prices went up 0.6% from August.
Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up slightly in September.

Overall price increases have largely driven by the US-Israel war with Iran, which has caused energy prices to soar. Average gas prices remain over a dollar per gallon more than last year, according to data from AAA. Meanwhile diesel, which powers domestic supply chains, reached a record-high last month.
September’s inflation rate is the highest it has been before a midterm election, with the exception of the pandemic, since 1990.

The economy has consistently been cited as a top issue for American voters, as rising gasoline prices and persistent inflation have eaten into household budgets. Higher energy prices from the Iran war have cost Americans over $1,020 per household, according to Brown University, and a total of $133bn for all US consumers.

Much of the anger is expected to be directed at Republicans, who control Congress and the White House. According to a recent survey from Reuters/Ipsos, 78% of Americans blame the current Trump administration’s policies for inflation that is outpacing their earnings, including 57% of Republicans who support Donald Trump.
In recent weeks, Trump has attempted to downplay his administration’s role in price increases, pointing to the Iranian government as the cause of the squeeze.
On Tuesday, Trump posted on social media that Yemen’s Houthi group was attacking Saudi Arabia in a deliberate effort to affect the upcoming elections.

“They’ve emerged again, probably at the behest of Iran…in a very nasty way, hitting Saudi Arabia, and purposefully trying to drive up Oil Prices, probably prior to the U.S. Elections — NOT NICE,” he wrote.

Last month, the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023, citing elevated inflation. Higher rates affect the cost of borrowing money, including mortgage rates. The 30-year mortgage rate, applied to the most commonly used loans for home ownership, is up to 7.40%.

articles.title: Burnham says he wants to 'repair bridges' between Ukraine and US
articles.summary: It comes ahead of a meeting between the prime minister and President Zelensky at Downing Street.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said it is his job to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street.
It comes after President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel.

Asked about Trump's move during Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham resisted criticising the US president, saying he wanted to "be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together".
However, he stressed that Zelensky would not be leaving the UK "empty-handed", as he said further military and financial support would be drawn up in the coming weeks.
Burnham is expected to use the visit to promise further sanctions against Russia, while also announcing the UK will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.
The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
During PMQs, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey asked whether he agreed the diesel deal was "yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security".

In response, Burnham did not echo Sir Ed's condemnation of Trump, saying: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should at this moment in time be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."

The PM said he had spoken to Zelensky over the phone on Saturday "because I recognised it was another very dark and difficult moment for him as they contemplate a winter that will be severe for his people".

articles.title: Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
articles.summary:
Health minister says government ‘did not authorize’ Danish-led hepatitis B trial in babies backed by RFK Jr

Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns…

blocks.text: Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.

The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.

Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.
But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.

“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.

“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, ‌must ⁠strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.

He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).

The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year. Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight.”

Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.

In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.
Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neo-colonialist” and “damaging”.

“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”
It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.

Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”

It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The ​study has ⁠not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.

At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.

The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.

Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “cancelled or suspended.”
Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.

The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

articles.title: Ken Paxton stirs vaccines skpeticism to ingratiate himself with Maha movement
articles.summary:
Texas AG and US Senate hopeful announced inquiry into alleged conspiracy between pediatricians, vaccine makers and insurance firms

Ken Paxton, the attorney general of Texas and the…

blocks.text: Ken Paxton, the attorney general of Texas and the Republican candidate for the US Senate, is aligning himself with the Make America Healthy Again (Maha) movement by investigating pediatricians for giving vaccines – actions that could further restrict access to vaccines as deadly outbreaks unfold.

Paxton announced he would investigate an alleged conspiracy between pediatricians, vaccine makers and insurance companies in January, and at least one Texas pediatrician now says she is under investigation. Paxton linked his efforts to a campaign against vaccines from Donald Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and directly referenced the Maha movement in his announcement. The president endorsed Paxton’s Senate run in May.

Pointing to a sweeping collusion that “illegally incentivized” doctors to administer vaccines, Paxton alleges that the pharmaceutical and insurance industries were attempting to “bribe” medical providers.

He also launched an investigation into the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), accusing them in August of potentially recommending vaccines for financial gain – referencing a lawsuit the AAP filed earlier this year to halt sweeping changes to the childhood immunization scheduleand once again invoking Trump and Kennedy’s moves on vaccines.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump and Ken Paxton during a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, on 7 October 2026. Photograph: Mandel Ngan/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: A new law in Taxes makes it easier for parents to request school vaccine exemptions, as the rate of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccination falls in the state. Only 93.3% of kindergarteners in Texas are now fully vaccinated against measles.
Pediatricians are one of the lowest-paid medical specialties and “barely break even” on vaccines, said Marjan Linnell, a pediatrician and president-elect of the Texas Pediatric Society.

But Kennedy has made millions suing vaccine makers. He’s made at least $2.5m in referrals for lawsuits related to vaccine side effects to law firm Wisner Baum. He had a 10% contingency stake in a Gardasil vaccine lawsuit that reportedly settled for about $50m in June.

In Kennedy’s confirmation hearing to become HHS secretary, Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, asked Kennedy about these potential conflicts of interest and whether he would continue receiving money from lawsuits while overseeing (and after leaving) HHS. Kennedy initially said he would stop profiting from vaccine lawsuits, but he later filed an amended ethics disclosure saying he would give the money to one of his sons.

“I get reimbursed as little as $6 for giving a vaccine,” said Katherine Wells, director of Lubbock Public Health. Even when her health department receives vaccines for free from the state, it only receives about $13 for the costs of administering the vaccine.

“That does not cover the time of a nurse to talk to the parents, review the shot record, draw up the vaccine, give the injection, provide the education. It’s way more than six bucks for me to do that in a health department, and I’m a low-cost, low-overhead entity.”
Wells continued: “I’m taking a loss every time I give a vaccine, but it’s the right thing to do.”

blocks.caption: Robert F Kennedy Jr testifies during a budget hearing in front of the Senate appropriations committee on 21 April 2026.  Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Primary care doctors have high levels of trust, as does the AAP – with both ranked as more trustworthy than federal health agencies in a February survey.
“Pediatricians are beloved,” said Paul Offit, a vaccines expert at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “People see them as nice people trying to do the right thing.”
Offit continued: “I just think this war on pediatricians is not a winner. Ken Paxton, I think, is desperate. He very well may lose to Talarico, and this is a stupid, desperate thing to do.”

Despite their broad popularity, pediatricians have frequently been targeted by anti-vaccine activists – including recent claims from Children’s Health Defense that they’ve reported doctors in Lubbock to the Texas medical board for treating measles patients. The organization, which was previously led by Kennedy, also sued the AAP for racketeering on the same day that Paxton announced he would investigate pediatricians.

Kennedy has frequently criticized the healthcare system in America, decrying what he says are doctors who make decisions based on a “financial bonus” and “hidden incentives that corrupt medical judgment”, according to a video he posted on X in August 2025.
“Doctors are being paid to vaccinate, not evaluate,” Kennedy claimed, adding: “That’s not medicine. That’s coercion.”
after newsletter promotion

At least one pediatrician in Texas has received letters indicating they are being investigated by the attorney general’s consumer protection division about her records of vaccination, including “potential misleading or deceptive acts regarding incentives associated with the administration of childhood vaccines”, according to reporting from the New York Times.

The investigators are requesting details on every “reward, financial benefit, bonus, discount, return, rebate or other consideration” from vaccine makers, prompting the pediatrician to spend thousands in legal fees, the Times reported.
All pediatricians could be at risk of investigations, making the future of practicing pediatrics hazy.

blocks.caption: Cases of Measles are on the rise in west Texas as over 150 confirmed case have been seen with one confirmed death. Photograph: Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Texas already has a shortage of primary care,” Linnell said. Actions like these could worsen the health care shortage, she added. “If you’re going to be potentially threatened with a lawsuit that could close your business down, it’s yet another reason for people to not go into primary care.”
She worries about pediatricians at smaller practices who may be forced to choose between vaccinations and high legal and administrative fees.

“If you have a fear that you’re going to have to spend a bunch of money – potentially stop your practice or really take a financial hit, having to defend a lawsuit – then it could be conceivable that you won’t be able to offer children vaccines,” Linnell said.

Making it more challenging for children to get vaccinated will increase the risk of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib), and others, Linnell said. These are diseases she had never seen before, and she had hoped never to see them in her entire career – but now they are spreading throughout the country, at the same time that the way to prevent them is being undermined.
“Threats like this just feed into this fear,” Linnell said.

The accusations of financial gain are particularly puzzling because vaccines are expensive and time-consuming to maintain and administer, Linnell said. Staff are trained on how to administer them; storage is complicated, with special freezers that can’t ever lose power. A couple years ago, there was a freeze for five days, and the bridge to Linnell’s clinic was frozen, she said. Every vaccine in the freezer had to be thrown out. “All of those vaccines, our clinic had to pay out of pocket to replace,” Linnell said.
With vaccination, “in some cases, we barely break even”, she said. “It’s not something we would do if we didn’t think they were so critically important and so safe.”
She continued: “Vaccines are expensive, but they’re worth it. They are one of the best studied, safest things that we can do to keep kids in their communities, playing, going to school.”

articles.title: Brian Poe urges global stakeholders to back PH in protecting WPS
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Rep. Brian Poe of the FPJ Panday Bayanihan Party-List urged international stakeholders to support the Philippines in protecting the West Philippine Sea, saying the maritime…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Rep. Brian Poe of the FPJ Panday Bayanihan Party-List urged international stakeholders to support the Philippines in protecting the West Philippine Sea, saying the maritime dispute affects regional marine biodiversity, global commerce and the principle of free and open trade.

Speaking last Monday at the G1 Global Conference in Tokyo, with the theme “KYOSEI: Symbiotic Societies,” Poe called on representatives from around the world to recognize the West Philippine Sea as a shared concern.
“This is not just the Philippine problem. This is all of our problems because trillions of dollars’ worth of commercial industry flows through the West Philippine Sea,” Poe said.
He underscored the importance of protecting the region’s marine ecosystem, pointing to its biodiversity and the consequences of failing to safeguard it.

Poe also stressed that protecting the West Philippine Sea’s marine biodiversity is a shared responsibility, especially among Indo-Pacific countries, noting that the area’s rich marine resources are vital to the region and could be threatened without collective protection.

“So protecting that for free and open trade is important to all of us, which is why I said yes to being on this panel and why I’m here with you today. So I hope you take that into consideration,” Poe added.
Poe said the maritime situation has direct consequences for Filipino fisherfolk, whose livelihoods depend on access to traditional fishing grounds.

He cited incidents involving water cannons, overfishing, intimidation by larger vessels, and restrictions that make some fishers feel unsafe going to sea without the presence of the Philippine Coast Guard.

He also highlighted the importance of strengthening the Philippine Coast Guard’s capacity to protect the country’s maritime interests and fishing communities. Poe cited Japan’s support for the Coast Guard’s fleet and radar systems.

During the discussion, Jack McCain, founder and CEO of McCain Advisory, a Tokyo-based strategic advisory firm, emphasized the importance of international coordination in responding to maritime security challenges. He called for clear responsibilities and agreed procedures among regional coast guards.

“So making sure that both the Korean Coast Guard and the Japanese Coast Guard and the Philippine Coast Guard all have a set of responses and a set of responsibilities that is clear, delineated, non-provocative, but also everybody knows exactly what to do when they need to do something,” McCain said.
Japanese Congressman Keishi Abe highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation among countries in the Indo-Pacific and their international partners.
He also called for stronger ties between the Philippines and Australia.
“And also, we have to elevate the level of cooperation with the Philippines and Australia to the alliance level. This is the issue that we face in the 21st century,” Abe said.

Poe’s message at the conference underscored the importance of international cooperation in protecting maritime resources, safeguarding fishing livelihoods and maintaining open trade routes in the Indo-Pacific. /atm

articles.title: Bank of America fined $1.2bn for money laundering failures
articles.summary:
Third largest fine in US treasury’s history, due to failure to report suspicious activity, may affect third-quarter earnings

Bank of America (BAC.N), has been fined $1.21bn by US regulators…

blocks.text: Bank of America (BAC.N), has been fined $1.21bn by US regulators for widespread failures to detect ‌potential money laundering and other illicit activity, a penalty the bank said will hurt third-quarter earnings.

The treasury department said the fine, the third-largest in department history, is due to the bank’s failure to report more than $5bn in suspicious activity to the government, including $1bn that posed national security-related and other priority illicit finance risks.

“Financial institutions are on the ​front lines of protecting our economic and national security,” the treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, said in a statement. “When a bank of this size ​fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the ⁠entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks.”

The treasury said the bank “prioritized its revenues” in building compliance programs, and overly relied on inquiries ​from outside parties such as law enforcement and other financial institutions instead of its own internal controls.

The consent order requires Bank of America to hire an ​independent third party to review past transactions, identify suspicious activity that the bank failed to detect at the time, and report those transactions to FinCen.

“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” said a Bank of America spokesperson in a statement. “We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of ​employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised ​by our regulators.”

The spokesperson added that the bank’s third-quarter results due for release on Wednesday would include a non-tax-deductible charge of $1.2bn, which will reduce quarterly net income ‌by approximately ⁠17 cents a share.
Analysts have estimated adjusted EPS of $1.10, according to mean estimates compiled by LSEG, but that excludes one-offs like this fine.
Shares were down 2.7% in after-hours trading after closing the day down 1.1%.

The penalty is likely to add to negative investor sentiment and raise concerns about higher expenses and whether Bank of America can maintain its roughly $6bn quarterly share buyback pace, the UBS analyst Erika Najarian said in a note.
With earnings due ​on Wednesday, “we think shares likely underperforming at ​open,” she said.
She noted there ⁠was no asset cap, a regulatory penalty that would limit how large the bank could grow.

As part of the fine, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency levied a $750m civil ​penalty against the lender, the largest ever for the regulator, citing failures to address shortcomings in its anti-money ​laundering programs that were ⁠identified as part of a 2024 cease-and-desist order from the watchdog.

The regulator said the bank’s compliance program was “deficient and ineffective”, and its transaction monitoring system caused the bank to delay filing suspicious activity reports on billions of dollars of transactions.

In addition, the bank paid an $11.6m fine to the Office of Foreign ⁠Assets Control ​for over 400 apparent violations of numerous sanctions programs. The treasury said the bank mistakenly ​processed millions of dollars in payments that violated sanctions programs targeting countries including Russia and Iran.
The fine comes days after American Express was also hit with a $350m penalty for similar anti-money ​laundering shortcomings.

articles.title: China's influence in the gaming industry is growing
articles.summary: Home to more than 700 million gamers, China is the world's largest gaming market — but it's also one of the most tightly regulated. The effects reach far beyond China, impacting players around the…

image.caption: The Chinese game 'The Defiant' is set during the Second Sino-Japanese WarImage: 4Divinity

blocks.text: In a dark underground hideout, dim light spills from a handful of oil lamps. A comrade fiddles with a rifle. A red flag hangs on one of the roughly hewn stone walls, bearing a hammer and sickle on a white star — the symbol of the ChineseWorkers' and Peasants' Red Army. Weapons are scattered on the ground. One is picked up, and soon the action moves into the snowy forest, where gunfire erupts among the trees.

Such a scene could fit in a new installment of "Call of Duty," the popular first person shooter game that transports players to battlefields past, present and future. But it is actually from "The Defiant." The game is currently being developed by the Chinese studio Hoothanes Technology in Hangzhou. It tells the story of Chinese forces fending off the Japanese army in the 1930s and 1940s.

Developer Connor Xu tells DW the weapons featured in the game are unique. They were used only in Asia and are therefore unfamiliar to many Western players, he says. The same goes for the story, which Xu says has never before been told in a video game.

blocks.caption: Game developer Connor Xu wants to tell stories from Chinese historyImage: Kristina Reymann-Schneider/DW

blocks.text: "The Defiant" is also designed to appeal to an international audience. In just a few years, China has emerged as a major player in the global gaming industry despite strict regulations, censorship and a former ban on video game consoles.
Gaming is part of everyday life in China

More than 700 million people in China regularly play video games. According to market research company Newzoo, most consider gaming an important part of their lives. Many use games to stay in touch with friends.

"Games make life more interesting," developer Xu says. "I can try different roles, different stories, different characters, because we only have one life to live, but we can play a role in another story. That's really attractive, I think, to Chinese users."

blocks.caption: 'Honor of Kings' is largely unknown outside China, but it's one of the country's most popular gamesImage: Tencent/Level Infinite/TiMi Studio Group

blocks.text: People in China primarily play games on PCs and smartphones, while consoles are much less common. There are historical reasons for that: While gamers in Europe and North America debated whether PlayStation or Xbox was the better console in the early 2000s, the devices were not officially sold in China between 2000 and 2014. Chinese authorities said the restrictions were intended to protect children and teenagers from becoming addicted to gaming.
Limits on gaming time and extensive controls

Minors in China are currently allowed to play online games for no more than three hours a week. There are no such limits for adults, but gaming is subject to strict controls. Anyone who wants to play must register using their real name and a personal identification number. That effectively allows the state to track who plays what and when, as well as whom they communicate with.

There is also a gray area that the Chinese government appears to tolerate. Some players log in using VPNs, giving them access to games that are not officially available in China. Some younger players use their parents' accounts to get around the limits on gaming time.

blocks.caption: The Chinese role-playing game "Genshin Impact" bears visual and gameplay similarities to "The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild"Image: Cognosphere/miHoYo/HoYoverse

blocks.text: Despite its strict controls on underage gamers, China has become increasingly receptive to video games in general, having recognized the industry's enormous economic potential. Early on, games released for Chinese players often appeared to be copies of Western titles. At the same time, Chinese tech companies such as Tencent and NetEase invested in numerous Western gaming companies.
No license? No sales in China

One distinctive feature of the Chinese market is its licensing system. "Unlike a lot of the other big video games markets in the world, China has a tightly regulated and licensed official video games market," George E. Osborn tells DW. The journalist advises NGOs and governments on video games and spoke at the Gamescom congress. In his book "Power Play," he describes how authoritarian states use video games to pursue political objectives.

blocks.caption: The strategy game 'Heroes of Might and Magic III Remake' is currently being developed by Ubisoft's studios in Chengdu and ShanghaiImage: Ubisoft

blocks.text: The rule for all games in China is simple: No license, no sales. "That system essentially forces developers who want to release their video games to go through multiple layers of approval from China's Ministry of Propaganda, Ministry of Culture," Osborn says.
Strict criteria for video games

Games are prohibited from containing material that threatens China's unity, sovereignty or territorial integrity, among other restrictions. Pornographic content and gambling are also banned. Games may not incite crimes that threaten national security or spread information authorities believe could disrupt public order.

"The whole point around this criteria is that it's deliberately designed to be pretty vague," Osborn says. Whether a game violates the rules is a matter of interpretation. Sometimes games are altered even after release. In the 2025 action role-playing game "Wuchang: Fallen Feathers," for example, enemies based on famous Chinese figures from the Ming Dynasty suddenly could no longer be killed. Instead, they would collapse from exhaustion.
Chinese culture is an international hit

The Chinese action role-playing game "Black Myth: Wukong" became an unexpected international hit in 2024. By then, it was clear Chinese developers could do more than cater to the domestic market — they could create successful games for a global audience as well. The game was inspired by the 16th-century Chinese literary classic "Journey to the West."

blocks.caption: The video game 'Black Myth: Wukong' became an international hitImage: Game Science Interactive Technology Co

blocks.text: Osborn sees nothing wrong with bringing Chinese culture to audiences around the world. The question, he says, is how much the state actually intervenes in the games themselves. "I think in general, video game players are actually quite deeply skeptical of these kinds of things. They are generally very good at spotting when someone might be selling to them or someone might be propagandizing. And so I think if it's too obvious, it won't work," he says.
The problem of self-censorship

Because of the licensing system, Western developers also have to comply with government requirements if they want to sell their games in China. And they do want to, Osborn says, because the market is too big to ignore. "But I think when you start thinking about the potential impact this has on creative standards around the world, I think it's really important that developers ask themselves the question of what will we or won't we compromise on here?"

He fears the real danger lies in self-censorship. That could lead developers, for example, to leave queer characters out of their games. That would represent a major step backward, he says, because games help many people explore their identities.

China is not the only country where games are modified to comply with national regulations. In Germany, for example, symbols that violate the country's constitution, such as the swastika, may not be shown in games unless the game in question explicitly contributes to the country's culture of remembrance. Depictions of extreme violence also have to be removed from German versions.
History from a Chinese perspective

Glorifying violence is prohibited in China, too, yet Xu's team is still allowed to develop a war game. How does this add up? Xu explains it this way: "I think in this game, the most important thing is not violence. The most important thing is to tell history."
Xu says the team is committed to delivering a historically accurate product. Whether it succeeds will be for historians to judge.
This article was translated from German and edited by Sarah Hucal.

articles.title: Mauritius reels from worst riots in decades after woman shot by police
articles.summary: Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam imposed a curfew after days of unrest that first began over water shortages.

blocks.text: Police in Mauritius imposed an overnight curfew overnight to quell the worst riots to break out on the Indian Ocean island in decades.
Peaceful protests over water shortages and the high cost of living that started a week ago erupted into violence on Friday when a woman was shot and wounded by police at a roadblock.
The circumstances of the shooting are not clear, but the officer has since been arrested and remanded in custody.
Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam ordered the curfew on Tuesday, warning against those "acting against the interests of the country", which is a tourism and financial services hub.
"Those who have carried out these actions will have to face the very heavy consequences warranted by their anti-patriotic acts," he said in an address to the nation.
Protesters burned tyres and blocked ‌roads as the unrest escalated over the weekend, with police stations and other public infrastructure properties being vandalised.
The mayhem prompted the closure of schools and public transport, with foreign embassies issuing alerts warning its nationals to be cautious.
Despite the curfew, police said there had been several incidents overnight and some arrests.
But the police assured people that by Wednesday morning traffic was again moving throughout the island and said people should resume their normal activities.

When protests over the shortage of water initially started, the government had responded proactively by providing more water to households, according to Zoë McCathie, an analyst at South Africa-based Signal Risk.

The escalation had presented a more "unusual situation for the country's security situation", with the government resorting to closing schools and imposing a curfew, she told the BBC's Newsday programme.
"Protests to this scale and to this extent haven't been seen… since around 1999. So the government's response to this in that case is logical and is necessary," she said.

While the government had managed to "curtail the worst of the unrest" there was still a possibility that protests could return in some areas, with water shortages expected to persist until the rainy season in December, she said.
The cabinet is due to meet on Wednesday afternoon to reassess the situation and decide on the next steps.

Over 111,000 policemen will be deployed to enforce security across the country for the observance of All Saints' Day and All Soul's Day on November 1 to 2, more than doubling the manpower compared to last year.

According to a statement on Wednesday by the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), the Philippine National Police (PNP) will beef up security in cemeteries and other areas of convergence.

"The PNP will be deploying 111,582 [police personnel] in 5,628 cemeteries and columbaria," Police Colonel Amante Daro, PNP acting executive officer-Directorate for Operations, said during a DILG forum on Wednesday.
The DILG statement said, "This year's deployment is higher than the police mobilization of over 50,000 cops in last year's Undas."

Of the deployed cops, 11,782 will be personnel from other units. Meanwhile, 31,814 will be force multipliers, including Barangay Peacekeeping Action Teams, PNP advocacy support groups, and local government unit employees who will assist in traffic management.

Aside from cemeteries, there will also be cops stationed at bus terminals and other transportation hubs amid the expected exodus of travelers. Cops will be visible in malls and resorts, the DILG added.
There will also be police patrols in residential communities, the department said.

"May pupunta ng probinsya, iiwanan ang kanilang mga bahay. Minsan buong pamilya wala, so walang tao. Sisiguraduhin ng inyong kapulisan na papatrolyahan 'yon, to make sure na 'di sila mapapasok ng masamang loob, at hindi manakawan ang kanilang tahanan," said Daro.

(Some will go to the province and leave their homes unattended. Sometimes the whole family is away, so no one is left behind. Your police force will ensure that those areas are patrolled to make sure bad elements don't enter and steal from their homes.)

Millions of Filipinos are expected to flock to their home towns and provinces during the annual commemoration to pay respects to their dearly departed loved ones and to reunite with their relatives as well. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: FAST FACTS: What changed in final version of the under-18 social media ban bill?
articles.summary: The Senate-approved bill expands the proposed social media ban to online gaming services, requires government-issued IDs for age verification, and targets addictive platform features

blocks.text: FACEBOOK. Facebook app icon is seen on a smartphone in this illustration taken October 27, 2025
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
The Senate-approved bill expands the proposed social media ban to online gaming services, requires government-issued IDs for age verification, and targets addictive platform features

items: The Senate has approved Senate Bill No. 2424, which bans children under 18 from accessing high-risk digital services, including social media, with stricter age verification requirements.

The bill expands coverage to include various high-risk digital services and mandates government-issued IDs for age verification, raising concerns about online anonymity and access for adults without proper identification.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate has approved a bill seeking to ban children below 18 from accessing social media and other digital services considered high-risk, introducing stricter age verification requirements and new obligations for technology companies, with a copy of the bill made available online this week.

Senate Bill No. 2424, or the proposed Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act, takes a stricter approach than the House of Representatives’ version, which proposes restrictions for children aged 13 and below and tiered access for older minors.
A comparison of the original proposal and the Senate-approved bill reveals six major changes.
The original proposal sought to prohibit children below 16 from accessing age-restricted social media platforms.
The approved version raises the age threshold to 18. The new version also explicitly states that the prohibition cannot be overridden by parental consent, authorization, or supervision.
So this means even 16- and 17-year-olds would be barred from covered platforms, with no provision for graduated access for older teenagers.
The approved bill introduces the term “high-risk digital services,” covering social media platforms and online gaming services with social networking functions.

These include features allowing users to communicate, maintain social connections, join online communities, or share user-generated content, including livestreams. Roblox and Gorebox are explicitly cited as examples.
These two games were tagged as potential avenues for youth radicalization and violent behavior; Roblox for its communication functions, and Gorebox for its supposed violent content.
However, the bill exempts email, certain private messaging services, educational platforms, digital news services, and professional collaboration tools.

There is also no minimum audience size or revenue threshold for coverage. Smaller livestreaming platforms and online communities could therefore be subject to the same requirements as major technology companies.

Unlike the original proposal, which allowed various age-assurance methods, the approved bill requires primary authentication through PhilSys or another government-issued ID. Age estimation and other verification technologies may supplement, but cannot replace, government ID authentication.

Simply entering a birthday would no longer suffice. As a measure of data minimization, platforms are prohibited from retaining copies of government IDs and should receive only information that users meet the age requirement.
Nevertheless, this requirement raises questions about online anonymity, surveillance risks, and access for adults without acceptable identification documents.

The new version introduces requirements for platforms to mitigate potentially addictive design features, specifically mentioning autoplay, infinite scrolling, push notifications, engagement metrics, and algorithmic amplification, also requiring “safety-by-design” and “privacy-by-default” protections.

However, it does not specify how exactly such mitigation can be enforced nor does it delve into technical benchmarks for determining whether these features have been sufficiently mitigated. The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) will be tasked with monitoring for compliance.
Violating platforms face fines ranging from P5 million to P20 million per violation, with additional daily penalties of up to P100,000 for continuing violations.
The approved bill requires platforms to take immediate, proportionate action against harmful content following detection or credible reports.
Measures may include suspending livestreams, removing content, restricting its distribution, or stopping algorithmic amplification.

Foreign platforms must maintain an emergency escalation channel and designate a legal representative or authorized contact in the Philippines. Notably, the approved version drops the original proposal’s explicit requirement for foreign platforms to establish a physical local office.

The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) must petition a Regional Trial Court, through the Office of the Solicitor General, to restrict an entire platform — a change from the unilateral banning actions that the DICT has performed, highlighted by the controversial Discord ban.
However, the DICT may still issue account-specific disabling orders if continuing harm can be proven. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Family of man killed by tiger criticise online content after Trump reposts video
articles.summary:
Relatives of William Chapman say footage of attack shared online ‘deeply offensive’ and causing them ‘severe distress’

The family of a man killed by a tiger at a UK wildlife park have spoken…
articles.byline: Mark Brown North of England correspondent

blocks.text: The family of a man killed by a tiger at a wildlife park in the UK have spoken about their “severe distress” at the circulation of online media after Donald Trump reposted a video of the incident.
William Chapman, 23, was mauled to death after entering an enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, on Saturday.
His family described him as “bright, warm and engaging” and suffering from severe mental illness. They said online footage being shared was “deeply offensive” and causing them “severe distress”.
One of those to circulate footage was the US president who posted a video clip of the tiger attack to 13 million followers on his Truth Social platform on Tuesday.
The clip showed the tiger biting and clawing Chapman as he was sitting in the enclosure. At one point he wags his finger at the animal.
Trump signed the footage with: “Don’t ever mess with nature! President DJT.” It did not show Chapman being killed.
Later the president posted an AI-generated video of himself grinning and having fun by chasing and play fighting with the tiger. It is accompanied by the song The Lion Sleeps Tonight by The Tokens.
It features Trump copying the pointing gesture made by Chapman and ends with him and the tiger hugging.
Relatives of Chapman, in a statement released on Tuesday evening, said: “The family are utterly devastated by their loss and are struggling to come to terms with what has happened.
“The publication and circulation of deeply offensive media content is causing them severe distress at an exceptionally vulnerable time. We ask people to stop doing this.
“The family are hopeful that the relevant authorities will do their upmost to get to the bottom of why our amazing son did what he did.”

The statement continued: “William was a bright, warm and engaging young man whom his family dearly loved – and William loved them back. Sadly, William suffered from significant mental illness over a number of years and was consequently prescribed strong medication.
“It will be for the coroner to decide what part this played in his death.
“We would ask everybody to respect that process.”
As a child, Chapman appeared in ITV’s 2009 comedy drama May Contain Nuts and in BBC Learning’s True Stories series, according to IMDb.
He previously attended Jackie Palmer stage school in High Wycombe, Buckinghamshire, which paid tribute on Facebook and posted a picture of Chapman as a child student.

The school said it was “deeply saddened” by Chapman’s death, adding: “We loved watching William grow, both as a person and as a performer. It was a privilege to be part of his journey, and he will be remembered with great fondness by everyone who had the pleasure of knowing him.
“William will be truly missed, and he will always hold a special place in our hearts. Rest in peace, William.”

The wildlife park has said the Amur (Siberian) tiger who was in the enclosure, called Altai, will not be euthanised. The park has remained closed since the weekend and Doncaster city council, which is responsible for licensing the park, said it had started a health and safety investigation.
An inquest is due to open into the death at Doncaster coroner’s court on Thursday morning.

articles.title: Ukraine says Musk's SpaceX limits Kyiv's Starlink access
articles.summary: Ukraine accused SpaceX of restricting use of its Starlink system, impacting Kyiv's ability to control its drones as Russian attacks continue unabated.

image.caption: Ukraine depends on Starlink for communications, logistics and drone operationsImage: Andriy Andriyenko/Ukrainian Armed Forces/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office confirmed on Wednesday that the country's military has been cut off from full access to SpaceX's Starlink satellite system as it seeks to defend itself against a now nearly five-year Russian invasion.
Russia launched an unprovoked, illegal, full-scale invasion of neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022.
"Tonight SpaceX introduced a speed limit for the Starlink terminals in motion," said Presidential Adviser Sergiy Beskrestnov.
"Our defence forces were not warned about this restriction, which led to the disruption of a number of missions," he added.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," he added.
Starlink cut-off coincides with Trump's 'energy ceasefire'

That political situation refers to US President Donald Trump's recent decision to extend Russian President Vladimir Putin a lifeline by lifting sanctions, buying Russian oil and berating Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy — saying he needs to stop attacking Russian oil infrastructure and that he should be replaced because "he won't make a deal" with Russia.

Due to rising oil and gas prices brought on by the war in Iran, Trump has repeatedly lashed out at the Ukrainian president, demanding he halt attacks on Russian energy facilities even as Russia continues to target Ukraine's civilian energy infrastructure to terrorize the country's citizens as winter approaches.
Trump has insisted, without providing evidence, that Russia and Ukraine have agreed to an "energy ceasefire." But Moscow and Kyiv have both denied this.
On Tuesday evening, for instance, Russian ballistic missiles hit a Kyiv power plant. Ukrainian officials said the Starlink outages had coincided with overnight Russian attacks.
Will Elon Musk give Ukraine Starlink's eyes over Russia?
SpaceX decision has impacted Ukraine's ability to defend itself
Ukrainian troops use Starlink to conduct drone operations and internet terminals supplied by Elon Musk's company are key to operating long-distance strikes.

Presidential Advisor Beskrestnov said SpaceX had cut off access to its military-grade version of Starlink above 100 miles per hour (160 km/h), adding that Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, had been forced to cancel some missions.

"According to our ‌observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10–20 seconds at speeds of ‌just 110–120 ​km/h. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," a Reaction Corps representative told Reuters news agency.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said such limitations significantly complicate logistics and ​drone operations.
Ukraine has used Starlink terminals as an alternative to radio control for its drones as well as for ground communications since shortly after Russia launched its invasion.
Starlink's resistance to electronic jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones as well as large hexacopters that drop supplies for Ukraine's frontline troops.
Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a key Donald Trump supporter, has, however, repeatedly shifted his stance on Ukraine since the early days of Russia's invasion.
In August, Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Kyiv was looking to create an alternative to Musk's Starlink, in concert "with a European country."

articles.title: Trump's US Super Intelligence Force and AI czar Jay Clayton
articles.summary: Trump announced a new Super Intelligence taskforce with the White House AI czar Jay Clayton in charge of a group responsible for making sure the US leads international competition in artificial…

image.caption: Donald Trump (left) named Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton (right) as his AI CzarImage: Alex Brandon/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: "Bigger than the Industrial Revolution and the internet" — US President Donald Trump used a comparison borrowed from "many others" to describe artificial intelligence (AI) in his announcement of a "Super Intelligence Force."

The president's move to address the rapid development of the AI industry came after he met with top AI executives at the end of September — and a month before midterm elections in November. Trump has faced intensifying pressure and warnings from business and political leaders about the mostly unregulated technology.

The name echoes Trump's September executive order renaming "Artificial Intelligence" as "Super intelligence" (SI). Jay Clayton, the director of national security and the president's new AI czar, is the task force leader.

The task force will coordinate the government's effort "to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence," Trump said, and "will protect the interests, and improve the lives, of all Americans."
How US, China could end the AI race
Trump has made it clear he does not want regulation to "stifle" progress in the SI industry, and a reported charter for the group says it will work to prevent "overregulation and regulatory capture."
What the Super Intelligence Force will do

The White House has not released any information about the Super Intelligence Force, but a copy of a charter detailing the group's responsibilities was reported in The Wall Street Journal and Politico.

The reported document shows the task force's scope is broad, but it names biosecurity and threats to the water supply as areas of focus. Recent cyberattacks have targeted critical infrastructure in the US.
Who is trying to hack the US water supply?

The group is to work with some of the most important US government agencies, including the Pentagon, the Justice Department, the Department of Homeland Security and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC), to develop recommendations for new laws to improve government responses.
A legal requirement for AI labs to notify the government of "breaches, hacks and jailbreaks" is to be considered, as well as the potential for automatic alerts.

"Though the labs are ultimately responsible for the risks and opportunities that their models amplify and accelerate, it is the role of the federal government to recognize and understand this era of change and to enforce our nation’s laws so that the fundamental principles of our Republic are safeguarded and advanced," the reported document says.

The charter's remit includes financial services, energy infrastructure, transportation, agriculture and emergency services. Trump said the task force would coordinate the government's engagement with consumers, public interest groups and religious organizations, as well as critical infrastructure providers and AI companies, though some critics noted the omission of workers.

The task force has 120 days to deliver a report on the risks of AI, focusing on potential threats to civil liberties, cybersecurity, standards for advanced models and the impacts of possible overregulation.

blocks.caption: Jay Clayton has been named the chair of Trump's newly announced Super Intelligence Force (SIT)Image: Ken Cedeno/AFP

blocks.text: Who is on the Super Intelligence Force?

Clayton, whom Trump named AI czar in early October, is to chair the task force. He told The Wall Street Journal he expected AI mechanisms to be "developed in dialogue," citing risk models the Securities and Exchange Commission, which he headed during Trump's first presidential term, and the Federal Reserve developed for the financial industry.
The reported charter also named three task force vice chairs:

items: Andrew Ferguson, chairman of the FTC
Emil Michael, undersecretary of defense for research and engineering
Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management

blocks.text: Ferguson is expected to oversee consumer interests and advocacy groups, according to the reported charter. His inclusion comes as the FTC investigates OpenAI, Anthropic and METR over rogue AI agents with potentially nefarious agendas.

Michael, a former tech consultant who sat on Perplexity AI's advisory board, is to oversee coordination with AI companies. Kupor is responsible for coordination with critical infrastructure providers and other industry stakeholders.

Key members of Trump's Cabinet, including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, are also on the task force. The reported charter also listed David Sacks, Trump's former AI czar, and Condoleezza Rice, former secretary of state under President George W. Bush, as external members.

blocks.caption: Former White House AI Czar David Sacks, seen here at the 2024 Republican National Convention, is reportedly an external participant in Trump's new Super Intelligence taskforceImage: Ron Sachs/CNP/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The task force is to report findings and recommendations to Trump and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.
Response to the task force

According to Politico, several key Republicans were not briefed on plans for the Super Intelligence Force before Trump's announcement. The task force comes as leading Republican Senators prepare major AI legislation intended to mitigate the risks AI poses.

Democrats have criticized the president, with Lori Trahan, a member of the House of Representatives, telling CNN that Trump was "just talking about an AI force without any sort of durable strategy on how to do that through congressional authorization," which felt more like a delay tactic.
"We should be passing legislation and guardrails around the frontier labs. And this doesn't do any of that," Trahan said.
Josh Gottheimer, another Democratic representative, told Politico he was also skeptical of Trump's motives.

"If this is the president waking up, realizing that AI risks aren’t a hoax, and is taking concrete action to protect America, then great," Gottheimer said. "If this is just a PR diversion and an attempt to protect his family’s investments, then I have a massive problem."
