blocks.text: One person has died and several others were injured after an incident on a rollercoaster at an amusement park in the US state of Georgia.

Six Flags Over Georgia park officials said staff found the man, identified as 42-year-old Atlanta resident Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, beneath the ride. He was unresponsive and not breathing. Witnesses have described the incident and its aftermath, with one man who was also on the ride describing it as "super bizarre, traumatic".

articles.title: Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story
articles.summary: Simbarashe Kundizeza was responding to an accusation that has caused an uproar on social media.

blocks.text: Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing.

His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.
"For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X, external.
The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing.

"I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme.

The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI, external - had been published on Sunday.

It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.
Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong.
The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.
Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being "crazy, racist and wildly unethical", external.
Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk", external.
Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised.
"There's something incredibly sinister about this," the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X, external.
"Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added.

Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025, external.
In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development.
Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original.
She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was "against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case".
Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested".
"I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready."

Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate".

In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels, external, which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to English-language writing by non-native English speakers.
The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation".

Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

"I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both."

In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing."
For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts.
"Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother.
"The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI.

The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.
He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.
"Much like the father in the story, my own dad... was an accountant, but he quit his job to grow tomatoes. So it kind of touches on both of our fathers," he told BBC Newsday.
On X, Kundizeza said he was heartened by "the numerous messages of solidarity from fellow writers and readers", ending his message by saying: "Most importantly, I will continue to write."

articles.title: Cornell suspends frat parties after gang rape case
articles.summary: Cornell said no parties will be held at frat houses until the end of the academic year. The university is trying to mend its reputation following its handling of a gang rape case in 2024.

image.caption: Cornell University will take several measures in response to the 2024 gang rape caseImage: Ted Shaffrey/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Cornell University has suspended all parties at frat houses until the end of the 2026/27 academic year, the university announced on Tuesday.

This comes after the case in which a woman alleged to have been drugged and sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, with the university's reaction to the gang rape allegations now attracting criticizm from around the nation and overseas.
The new measures include a new "zero tolerance" policy for violations, which would result in an immediate suspension of a chapter.

University President Michael Kotlikoff said these measures were to "provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life" at Cornell, while also determining how it can safely continue. The university has more than 20 active fraternities that are organized under its Interfraternity Council.
It is not clear whether the suspension also includes parties that take place outside the campus.
More support for victims

As part of the measures, Cornell is to hold talks with students and faculty experts about the "the development of safe social alternatives" to Greek life party culture, as well as investing the money needed to support the initiatives' establishment, Kotlikoff said.
The Cornell president also said the institution will be adding a case manager to its Office of Civil Rights to support people that report sexual misconduct to help in navigating the process.

Campus police, which has full law enforcement authority but is controlled by Cornell, are largely the ones responsible for looking into crimes committed at the university. However, Kotlikoff announced that Cornell will work closely with New York State Police to allow an investigation independent of the school.

blocks.caption: The case triggered widespread protests across the USImage: Melissa Bender/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Decision not to prosecute criticized

The 2024 gang rape allegations were initially investigated by the campus police, which then passed its initial findings to the Tompkins County district attorney, who did not prosecute — a decision that was lader met with widespread criticizm.
The woman filed a lawsuit in September, in which she claimed she had been drugged and sexually assaulted by several fraternity members after attending a party at the Chi Phi house in October 2024.
According to the lawsuit, messages saying she was sexually available were sent among fraternity members without her knowledge.

blocks.caption: The Chi Phi fraternity house, where the woman was allegedly assaultedImage: Heather Ainsworth/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: After learning about the case, Cornell closed the fraternity chapter and disciplined several students, without any criminal charges being filed.
All seven men mentioned in the lawsuit have denied the allegations.

After the case was made public and triggered wide-scale criticism, the investigation is now in the hands of New York Attorney General Letitia James. The university's response will be reviewed by former Deputy US Attorney General Sally Yates.

articles.title: Pakistan has locked down Imran Khan's stronghold - but it could backfire
articles.summary: Some fear the government's standoff with the former PM's supporters could bring more instability, not less.

blocks.text: Schools closed. The internet partially shut. Roads blocked by shipping containers. And the army arriving in town.

Imran Khan's party stronghold, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, is under a state of emergency, his party's provincial government suspended. It's another dramatic escalation in the standoff between the former prime minister's supporters and Pakistan's state - and one that some fear could lead to more instability, not less.
According to the federal government this step, allowed by the constitution, was needed to provide protection for the province's population from the threat of terror.

"The PTI KPK government was hand in glove with the terrorists," Attah Tarrar, federal information minister, told journalists on Sunday. He did not elaborate or provide evidence, but promised to do so soon.
Two days later there had still been no update from him - but schools had reopened in Peshawar and most parts of the province, and internet services had been restored.
While police would not confirm any detentions, there is clearly a crackdown under way to prevent protests. Most PTI leaders in the province have gone into hiding.
On Tuesday dozens of PTI supporters took to the streets in Bara, Khyber district, hometown of provincial Chief Minister Sohail Afridi. There were reports of tear gas shelling in the area.
To many observers, the timing of Sunday's announcement of emergency rule is not coincidental.
For the last week, thousands of Imran Khan's supporters have marched through Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, where the PTI have been in power for 13 years, demanding Khan's release.
"The charitable response would be to say that it sounded disingenuous," says Farzana Sheikh, associate fellow at Chatham House.

"I do not see the link with terrorism," says Arifa Noor, journalist and commentator. "I'm not even sure if it was the long march itself [that led to this]. Perhaps it was the last straw or perhaps it's just a case of saying, we don't want to deal with the government being in the hands of an opposition party."
The protests were led by Chief Minister Afridi, whose whereabouts are still a mystery. His party says he has been arrested; the government says that he is in protective custody.
Before the march had begun, there had been a crackdown. Three of Khan's sisters were arrested in September, accused among other things of mobilising supporters, and have been detained ever since.

Khan has barely been seen by his family or lawyers in the last year; two of his sisters saw him in August, one in prison, another as he was checked over at a hospital visit after concerns were raised by the Supreme Court about his health, before he was returned behind bars again where he has been held for more than three years.

The PTI leader, who is widely believed to have lost power because of a rift with Pakistan's powerful military, has been imprisoned since August 2023. He is convicted in several corruption cases which he says are politically motivated.
With the party already weakened, why this reaction from the authorities?

"The PTI rank and file has been becoming increasingly restless in recent months amid growing concerns about Imran Khan's health," says Michael Kugelman, senior South Asia fellow at the Atlantic Council.
"There is a sense that perhaps now is the time to send a very strong message to the party and make it more difficult for them to be able to put pressure on the government."
The government has previously argued that Khan was going against jail rules by using his meetings to discuss politics.

Tarar has said of the state of emergency: "There was no political agenda. They could have gone on with their march," and pointed to the talks the two sides had in the run-up to the decision as an indicator that they did try discussion.
But others see this as just another attempt to restrict Khan and his party.
"The government has less and less space for disagreements or dissent and they do not want to negotiate their way out of any kind of conflict," Noor says.
Zahid Hussain, Islamabad-based author and defence analyst, is clear about who is behind the decision.
"The balance of power is completely shifted to the military establishment," he says.

Sheikh thinks that Pakistan's military is feeling confident because it believes it has a good relationship with the White House, its international credentials burnished by their role in the US-Iran peace talks.
"The mode is very much, this is the moment, let's seize it," she says. "There is a sense that, we have all the cards in our hands. We can ride this out internationally."
But Pakistan has plenty to contend with. Militancy is rising. The country was ranked number one in the Global Terrorism Index 2026 as the country which had been affected most.

The country is at loggerheads with two neighbours; it has repeatedly hit Afghanistan with air strikes accusing the Afghan Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, a claim it denies. It would take little to reignite its long-running simmering conflict with India.
Meanwhile, it has promised to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against attacks as the conflict against the Houthis has become increasingly dangerous.

Short of solving one problem, some have warned this state of emergency could lead to more challenges. It risks increasing political instability, with Islamabad taking responsibility for a province without a buffer - the provincial government - they can blame.

"I would argue that this could actually backfire," Kugelman says. "You're playing with fire because if this move ends up adding to the anger and the discontent among so many there, then you have a very big problem on your hands."
"It is reckless, given the challenges, multiple challenges the country is facing," Hussain says. He fears that more of these powers could be used across Pakistan.
Attempts to combat militancy with more active army operations could come with its own perils too, Sheikh argues.

"If they're going to launch these operations, they're going to have to be prepared to accept casualties of members of the armed forces," she says. If those are significant, it could lead to questions inside the military institution, she adds.
Pakistan, with its history of military coups, has examples in its past where removing elected governments, whether provincial or national, can turn sour.
"It's not that senior people in the PML-N [the party in federal government] don't realise that some of these things can come back and haunt them in the future," Noor says.

"Similarly I think to some extent the PTI realises that they will not be able to hold a protest and get Imran Khan out. I think that's the most unfortunate part of this mess that we're in, that we are going into it with our eyes wide open.
"Everybody realises that this is a train crash but somehow you can't stop it."

articles.title: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
articles.summary: As loneliness grows in China, a new industry is emerging to provide companionship and support.

blocks.text: 'I'd talk to the TV': The paid companions bringing warmth to China's lonely
Watch: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
"The biggest difficulty really was the loneliness. Sometimes, if I wanted to talk to someone I'd talk to the TV."
Yang, 91, lives on the outskirts of China's bustling capital Beijing. Following the death of her husband, she was so lonely that she says she even considered the possibility of voluntary euthanasia.
"I asked my son about it but he told me it was banned. I told him that if it ever becomes legal I want to do it - I didn't want to live any longer."
Suffering glaucoma, with failing eyesight, she was unable to even do basic things like adjust the controls on her air conditioner.

Cases such as Yang's have become increasingly common in Chinese cities which Associate Professor Teresa Kuan, from the Chinese University of Hong Kong, says is "exacerbated by the structure of society and the modes by which people interact".

There are many causes of isolation in China. Most of it happens when rural migrants pursue economic opportunities, leaving behind close-knit support networks for urban centres where loneliness and uncertainty can be difficult to overcome, or when graduates uproot themselves chasing employment on the other side of the country.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.

blocks.text: Suffering from glaucoma and failing eyesight, 91-year-old Yang found simple tasks and daily life increasingly difficult on her own.
But now a growing "loneliness industry" has emerged to try to fill these gaps in people's lives.

Yang says her life has been transformed by one of these services - Wang Yingwei and his electric scooter delivery team - who started coming over twice a day with hot meals but whose help extends far beyond that.
"We see ourselves as community children," Yingwei told the BBC. "It means putting yourself in the shoes of older people and carefully considering their needs.

"For example, they may be drinking tap water which can be cloudy and contain a lot of lime. I can fix this problem with a filtered water tank. Such a small thing can make them much happier. Maybe they can't shower because their equipment is broken. I'll buy a part, replace it and their shower is fine."
"The elderly treat us like their children, and we treat them like our own parents," he added.
Yingwei's services cost less than half the price of employing a caregiver.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.

blocks.text: Wang Yingwei and his small delivery team offer more than just meals, bringing human connection to elderly residents.

The former mobile phone salesman says he started his company to help seniors remain at home without having to move into retirement facilities. He was inspired to do this after his own father-in-law, who had developed Alzheimer's, had to go into a nursing home. Yingwei said he felt that the conditions there were so sub-standard he wanted to make sure others could stay out of institutions like this for as long as possible.
His small business currently employs four people but he says there is a possibility he will expand as demand grows.

There is still a shortage of solid data on the size of this sector – which operators say has exploded in recent years – but securities company Sinolink valued it at around $7.4 billion in 2025. And this is only expected to grow given the trajectory of modern lifestyles.
Zheng Ruizhi, another client of Yingwei's who lives in Beijing's northern outskirts, welcomed him at the door with a big smile.
"After retiring, I don't have much opportunity to hang out with others," the 75-year-old, whose son lives two hours away from her, told the BBC.
She was recovering from a recent injury which she said was making everyday tasks more difficult.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.

blocks.text: Zheng Ruizhi, 75, shares a lighthearted moment with Wang Yingwei during a home visit.
But the arrival of Yingwei – who she calls her "dear boy" – lightened her mood.

"I call you 'dear boy' because I am so fond of you. I genuinely like you from the bottom of my heart. I also admire and trust you. When you help me out, I don't have a single worry or fear," she told him.
Yet the services offered by those in this sector are not limited to home visits.

Twenty-three-year-old Liu Yanyan, for instance, works as a "medical escort". She acts as a friendly face taking clients to see the doctor, or picking up their test results or medication from city hospitals, which can be intimidatingly large and bureaucratic.

"Some of my customers are people in their 20s who came to Beijing to build a career. They might not have friends here or feel awkward asking colleagues to accompany them because of the concept of social reciprocity in Chinese culture," she said. "If I accompanied you to a doctor's appointment for free, you might feel obligated to buy me a meal or a movie ticket afterwards."
She said that, because of this, there are many people in modern Chinese society who tend to keep to themselves.
"So, they hire someone like me to accompany them to the hospital. If they had to go alone, they could feel scared or anxious."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.

blocks.text: Liu Yanyan, a 23-year-old medical escort, helps clients navigate complex city hospitals.
At the core of many businesses catering to loneliness in China is a simple offering: human connection.
Teresa Kuan said that some people prefer the option of pouring their hearts out to a complete stranger for a fee.

"If there is a companion you have paid for, the relationship is not exactly equal. It is a service relationship, so you don't have to deal with the unpredictability of a standard relationship. The thing about friendship is that it can be unpredictable. You don't know when someone might disappoint you. But, in a service relationship, you have a better idea of what to expect."
Wang Zhoutao runs a hiking business to help people who want to climb China's famous mountain Huangshan in Anhui Province.
"We provide emotional support, like cheering them up, taking their photo or telling jokes. It's really a service based on companionship," he said.
The former soldier added that he normally hikes up the mountain with clients 10 to 15 days a month. When fully booked, this could be as many as 30 times a month.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.

blocks.text: Mountain escort Wang Zhoutao guides a client up the steep steps of Mount Huangshan.
He gave an example of a young woman he once accompanied who felt ostracised at work. "She felt useless and wanted to prove something to herself," he said.

"We started climbing but it was a tough trek as the weather was really hot and we were sweating a lot. There were moments she wanted to give up but I told her, 'If you quit now and can't get over this mountain how will you handle anything else in life?'. I kept encouraging her."
After they made it all the way he said she sent him a long message of thanks describing her inner journey and expressing her gratitude.

"The pace of life is just too fast these days. People face pressure from work, relationships and family expectations," he said. "I think my clients are mostly people who feel a void in their relationships or have suffered a setback."
Human connection is a necessity but, in a society grappling with loneliness across generations, it has now also become a commodity.
Back in her little Beijing flat, Yang is feeling more comfortable now that Yingwei has sorted out her problem of making the air conditioner work properly.
"It's good to have someone around when you need it, someone you can share your innermost thoughts with," she said.
"I did struggle with loneliness but that's been resolved now. I'm quite happy.
"I can't lose Yingwei and the others. They've all got a good heart."

articles.title: Who's to blame for the toxic smog choking South East Asia?
articles.summary: Anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning land in Indonesia and the authorities who have failed to stop them.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Wildfires have been raging in Kalimantan, Indonesia for weeks
ByKoh Ewe
Reporting fromSingapore
As Indonesia battles its worst wildfire season in a decade, a toxic smog is choking millions of residents in the region.
The air on the islands of Kalimantan and Sumatra have turned an ominous amber, with air quality recorded at hazardous levels.

The smog - also known as the haze - has also drifted beyond Indonesia's borders to neighbouring countries, raising public health concerns. It has obscured Singapore's skyline and forced some schools to close in Malaysia.
Now, anger is mounting at the companies accused of burning farmland - as well as the authorities who have struggled to stop them.
The annual dry season wildfires have been especially intense this year because of an unusually strong El Niño - a natural climate phenomenon which changes weather patterns around the world.
According to independent forest monitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, 1,043,377 wildfire hotspots have been recorded in Indonesia, burning a total of 900,000 hectares of land.
Slash and burn
Many of these fires in Indonesia's forests and peatlands are caused by the razing of vegetation to clear land - a practice known as "slash and burn".
This is an agricultural method that has traditionally been employed by farmers in Indonesia to create nutrient-rich soil for new crops.

But today, many of these fires are associated with commercial farming and are taking place on a much larger scale - and are harder to control. Activists and government investigations have repeatedly accused some companies of using fire as a cheap way to clear large swathes of land.
While slash-and-burn farming is illegal in Indonesia, enforcement of a ban has long proven tricky.
But persistent haze this year has prompted Indonesian authorities to step up efforts to punish offenders.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has called for tougher sanctions against slash-and-burn farming, describing the practice as "ecological terrorism".

Last month, Indonesian authorities announced they had suspended the operating licences of 26 companies linked to the wildfires and launched investigations into others. Cases involving criminal elements would be taken to court, officials vowed.
But it's not just Indonesian companies that have been embroiled in controversy amid the haze problem.
Watch: What makes fires in Indonesia so hard to extinguish?
A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia which are linked to plots of land in Indonesia where wildfires are burning.

This includes First Resources, a Singapore-based palm oil company. Between August and September more than 30 haze source points were recorded on land managed by its two Indonesian subsidiaries, according to Greenpeace.

First Resources told the BBC in a statement that it maintained a "strict zero burning policy across all planting activities and implement robust fire prevention, monitoring and firefighting measures throughout our operations".
Greenpeace also named Malaysian plantation group Kuala Lumpur Kepong, whose subsidiary PT Menteng Jaya Sawit Perdana managed land in Indonesia where 19 haze source points were recorded.
Kuala Lumpur Kepong said in a statement that a "majority" of the fires originated from beyond its concession area and had all been extinguished.
"We do not condone or permit the use of open burning for land preparation or any other purpose across our operations," it said.
'When there is no smoke, we send oxygen'
It remains to be seen how effective governments can be in sanctioning offending companies.
In 2014, Singapore passed the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act which allows the government to take action against local and foreign firms found to be contributing to the haze.

The following year when Singapore saw a bad bout of haze, authorities issued summonses to several Indonesian companies thought to have cleared land by burning, in a bid to prosecute them under the new law.

But that drew sharp ire from Jakarta, which said the move harmed bilateral ties. And with Indonesia refusing to cooperate, Singapore authorities said they could not obtain information about the suspected companies.

Also in 2015, Indonesia's then-Vice-President Jusuf Kalla angered Singaporeans when he said that "for 11 months, they enjoyed nice air from Indonesia and they never thanked us... they have suffered because of the haze for one month and they get upset".

Similar tensions surfaced again last weekend when Syahganda Nainggolan, who leads Indonesia's government communications agency, said the raging wildfires were beyond human control and added that the oxygen in neighbouring Singapore and Malaysia "also comes from our forests".
"When there is no smoke, we send oxygen," he added, in a video that has been widely circulated on social media, triggering criticism and ridicule from Malaysians and Singaporeans.
Watch: Toxic smog makes thousands sick as Indonesia wildfires rage
But Indonesia has in the past also apologised to its neighbours for causing the haze.
This year, Indonesian officials have thanked Singapore and Malaysia for offering to help tackle the wildfires - though it has not officially requested international support.
In Indonesia, there have been efforts by civil society to force the government to take action.

In Pontianak in the West Kalimantan province, several groups have filed a class action lawsuit against the Indonesian government and Prabowo, accusing them of "gross negligence" over recurrent toxic haze.
They want the government to declare the haze a national disaster, which would allow for recovery measures such as the coverage of healthcare costs.
A similar case was filed last year in South Sumatra, but it was dismissed.
Meanwhile, on the ground in Kalimantan and Sumatra, air pollution levels have remained at dangerous levels for weeks.
There are many who have no choice but to brave the toxic smog every day.

"I'm short of breath and have a headache breathing air now. But I still have to work," Imrayedi, a 63-year-old motorcycle taxi driver in Pekanbaru city, on Sumatra island, told BBC Indonesian last week.
"The government must also think about the common people like us. Please take action to find a solution so that this haze problem can be resolved immediately."

articles.title: Why the lonely in China are hiring 'temporary children'
articles.summary: A new industry being dubbed the “loneliness economy” has emerged in China, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly.

blocks.text: In China's cities, despite the huge crowds, or maybe because of them, residents can feel very isolated.
Now, a new industry being dubbed the "loneliness economy" has emerged, with people hiring themselves out as companions to help the elderly.
The BBC's China correspondent Stephen McDonell visits a company that does just that, to see how their business works.

articles.title: Saudi man charged with planting 'sophisticated' recording device in OpenAI office
articles.summary: Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

blocks.text: A Saudi national has been charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's offices in California, federal prosecutors announced.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked at the AI firm as an engineer, was charged federally with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

OpenAI said it had discovered a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in their San Francisco office and alerted the FBI. The company said it used its AI models to track that it had been planted by an employee.
Prosecutors say the device, wrapped in toilet paper, was found inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.

OpenAI, the maker of the popular chatbot ChatGPT, said that it has no indication that source code, model weights or customer data were inappropriately accessed or taken in the incident. It said the employee has been fired.

According to the complaint, Alfozan "allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.
Patel said that the alleged goal was to capture information about the company's AI product.
Alfozan has been working as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, prosecutors say.
On 30 September, OpenAI employees discovered the device - two days after prosecutors say it had been installed. The device was encrypted, prosecutors said.
OpenAI said they were able to use their AI models "to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier".
According to the FBI, the suspect used a "productivity tool" and a "chatbot" to research sensitive locations at OpenAI and how to secretly place audio equipment.
Chatbot prompts that he is alleged to have searched include "building, customizing, installing, audio recording, testing, obfuscating, and remote accessing a device", prosecutors allege.

He is also accused of using the chatbot to ask about "'build[ing] a continuous audio recorder,' 'customiz[ing] Wi-Fi . . . connectivity,' 'improv[ing] audio and live listening,' and 'encrypt[ing] the SD card'".

articles.title: OpenAI says employee caught planting listening device
articles.summary: A Saudi national employed by the artificial intelligence lab has been arrested after a listening device was planted in a company conference room.

image.caption: A listening device was found late last month, OpenAI saidImage: Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, said Tuesday one of its employees was arrested after a "sophisticated recording device" was found in one of its San Francisco offices.

A 35-year-old Saudi national working as an engineer was arrested on Friday, a week after the device was discovered in a conference room, according to a criminal complaint filed in federal court in San Francisco.
After the device was discovered, the company reported the finding to the FBI and fired the employee. A federal investigation is ongoing.
The suspect, who appeared in court on Tuesday, has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.

The criminal complaint did not specify what the suspect might have wanted to do with the recordings. It did add, however, that the suspect used a tool to inquire about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, meeting-room capacities and calendars.
Will AI destroy humanity?
How was the device found?
OpenAI said the device was discovered a few days after it was allegedly planted by the suspect.

"We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," a spokesperson for the artificial intelligence company told the Associated Press.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," the spokesperson added.
According to the US Justice Department, the suspect wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and hid it inside a television located in an "executive conference room."

He was seen on camera near the room several times despite not having authorization to sit in meetings there. After this was noticed, another camera was installed in the room that captured the suspect on film checking on the stashed device.

articles.title: Alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant denied bail
articles.summary: Assistant United States attorney Todd Greenberg, who is prosecuting the case against Bryant, argued that Bryant posed a flight risk and a danger to the public. He said there were substance abuse…

image.caption: A district court judge in Seattle is set to hear arguments about whether alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant should be granted bail. (Lois Silver/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Assistant United States attorney Todd Greenberg, who is prosecuting the case against Bryant, argued that Bryant posed a flight risk and a danger to the public. He said there were substance abuse issues and mental health concerns that should also be factored in.
Seattle court heard arguments from lawyers on both sides
A district court judge in Seattle has refused bail for alleged Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator James Cody Bryant.

Bryant, a 30-year-old resident of Bellingham, Wash. — whose lawyers say uses she/her pronouns and goes by the name Melody — was arrested Oct. 6 and charged with one count of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.
Prosecutors say that conspiracy involved encouraging and supporting Tumbler Ridge Secondary School shooter Jesse Van Rootselaar in the lead-up to the attack.
On Feb. 10, Van Rootselaar killed five students and one staff member at the campus after shooting and killing her mother and half-brother at their home.
Police allege that in online interactions on the social media platform Discord, Bryant agreed to livestream the attack, gave Van Rootselaar money, and provided months of logistical support.
In making her ruling, Magistrate Judge Mary Alice Theiler described Bryant as having "serious mental health concerns" and substance abuse problems.
She added that release would require constant supervision to prevent Bryant from accessing the internet, something she did not believe authorities could achieve.
Bryant — dressed in prison greens — wept throughout the proceedings.
Assistant United States attorney Todd Greenberg, who is prosecuting the case against Bryant, had argued that Bryant posed a flight risk and a danger to the public.
The home of alleged Tumbler Ridge shooting co-conspirator James Cody Bryant in Bellingham, Wash. (Caroline Barghout/CBC)
"It does not get much more serious or dangerous for the community," he said in a memorandum filed Tuesday in support of a detention order.

"Bryant's participation in the charged murder conspiracy took place primarily through online communications … There are simply no conditions of release that can be fully and effectively enforced to ensure that Bryant does not pose a continuing threat to the community through online behavior."
Efforts to assist in shooting
Tuesday's memorandum drew on conversations alleged to have taken place between Bryant and Van Rootselaar as the attack was planned.

On Feb. 9, the day before the shooting, Van Rootselaar reportedly told Bryant she didn't want to carry out the shooting if she didn't "know for certain" someone would livestream it, the court documents outline.

items: Disturbing new details of Tumbler Ridge shooting plans revealed in court documents

blocks.text: "I literally fixed my sleep schedule to help me stay up to be there after work," Bryant replied.
According to the memorandum, a livestream was initiated in the moments before the attack but failed after about 20 seconds due to technical issues.
"The livestream's failure was despite Bryant's best efforts to make it happen," Greenberg said.

Greenberg also pointed to a payment of $14.33 Bryant sent to Van Rootselaar's PayPal ID to enable her to purchase a lighter to ignite an explosive device constructed for use in the attack. The payment was reversed because the account had been deactivated.
The District of Tumbler Ridge town hall as pictured on Aug. 21, 2026. (Tom Summer/CBC)
"Van Rootselaar ultimately deployed this explosive device," Greenberg said.

"Although $14.33 may not be a lot of money, it speaks volumes about the seriousness of the offense and the defendant's character that Bryant was willing to help purchase the ignition source for an explosive device that was to be used to attack schoolchildren."

He also argued substance abuse and mental health concerns should be factored in, including evidence of suicidal ideations that were shared with Van Rootselaar but not disclosed to the Probation Office.

items: U.S. resident's actions 'helped facilitate' Tumbler Ridge attack: RCMP asst. commissioner | Hanomansing Live

blocks.text: "Bryant repeatedly acknowledged being in a unique position to stop Van Rootselaar," he said.

"Anyone whose character allows them to help plan a mass shooting and then sits back and (literally) tries to watch as schoolchildren are murdered … is a danger to the community and should be detained pending trial."
Defence argues for conditional release

In their application opposing a motion for detention, assistant federal public defenders Gregory Murphy and Dennis Carroll argued Bryant had co-operated with investigators in the days following the attack.
"She expressed horror at Van Rootselaar's crimes," they said.
The defence argued that law enforcement had acknowledged Bryant repeatedly tried to dissuade Van Rootselaar from carrying out the attack, and pointed to their client's clean criminal record.
Accused Tumbler Ridge co-conspirator denied bail
"There is no evidence that she has ever personally committed an act of violence. There is no evidence that she is in contact with anyone else planning an act of violence," Murphy and Carroll said.
Defence counsel underscored Bryant's stable residence, close ties to the community, and long-term employment at a local McDonald's restaurant.
In his submission, Greenberg said Bryant had admitted to being "on thin ice" at work due to repeatedly calling in sick.

items: Alleged use of Discord to plan Tumbler Ridge shooting comes under scrutiny

blocks.text: "It's not clear whether that job remains available due to the arrest in this case," he said.

Murphy and Carroll also disputed Greenberg's mental health concerns, arguing that although Bryant had "briefly" seen a psychologist during high school and had taken medication for panic attacks, there was no evidence to support claims of suicidality.
"There is no evidence she has expressed a thought of harming herself in the last 14 months. There is no evidence she ever has made plans to hurt herself," the application read.
Corrections

items: A previous version of this story said Magistrate Judge Mary Alice Theiler described James Cody Bryant as a "tragically vulnerable, unstable individual." In fact, she was referring to Jesse Van Rootselaar. A previous version also referred to one of the victims as Van Rootselaar's stepbrother. In fact, he was Van Rootselaar's half-brother.Oct 13, 2026 6:47 PM EDT

items: 13m agoWelcome

blocks.caption: Ben Doherty

blocks.text: Ben Doherty
The Josh Frydenberg book-promotion/comeback-to-politics tour continues.
The former treasurer, and ousted member for Kooyong, appeared on 7:30 last night, again raising the possibility of his return to frontline politics.
His memoir, A Grateful Son, is the Trojan Horse that legitimises questions like: “Do you think you’d make a good prime minister?”

“Look, I haven’t closed the door to reentering politics,” Frydenberg reiterated. “That would involve running for a seat, winning it, joining the party room and then proceeding after that. So there are a lot of steps.”
He told host Sarah Ferguson that “if I was to run, it would be at the next election”, but insisted “it’s not a decision that I have taken”.
Full marks for persistence, Ferguson tried again: “Do you have what it takes to lead the country?”

Frydenberg: “Look, I think it’s important to know what you believe in, and I certainly do, to have policy ideas that can take the country in the right direction, and to be consistent with the philosophy and the values of our great party, and that’s what I articulate in the book.”

blocks.caption: Sarah Basford Canales

blocks.text: Sarah Basford Canales

Gas companies would be forced to set aside 20% of exports for Australian use under new legislation for a national gas reservation scheme to be introduced, with Labor committing to more transparency and tighter rules to prevent the system from being gamed.
The resources minister, Madeleine King, will introduce the amended bills that will give the Australian Energy Regulator the power to force companies to meet a target of 110% of demand each year.
It will also limit ministerial discretion and replace the Turnbull-era domestic gas security mechanism.

In a speech to be delivered at the National Press Club King will say a successful energy transition for the country will rely on a “guaranteed supply of affordable gas” for households, renewable energies and the processing of critical minerals and rare earths.
King will also say Australia must continue exporting traditional commodities, including gas and coal.

double quotation markNo two countries will follow exactly the same pathway to reducing emissions. What remains important is the commitment to the goal and a peaceful and inclusive journey toward it, so that we can minimise the damage caused by climate change, while making sure our communities have the energy they need.
Mark Dreyfus has fired off a warning to social media platforms about the livestream of US military execution planned for December.
The former attorney, who is now the special envoy for international human rights, said Australia held longstanding opposition to the death penalty and had raised it with the United States.

double quotation markAustralia opposes the death penalty in all circumstances, for all people ... the proposed livestreaming of an execution is deeply distressing. Platforms have a responsibility to prevent this disturbing content from being shown to Australians.
Yesterday, Anthony Albanese said he found the proposed streaming of a firing squad execution “completely abhorrent”, adding “we should do whatever we can to stop that occurring”.
The prime minister told ABC social media platforms risked harming their reputation for allowing streams of the execution but the government was limited in shutting them down.
Albanese said the government was receiving advice on its options. He said:
double quotation markIf there is something, anything we can do, we will do. I assure you of that.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has urged progressives not to disregard voters that are attracted to One Nation’s message in the Bernie Fraser oration at the Shine Dome in Canberra last night.
Chalmers said Pauline Hanson would be a disaster in government, calling One Nation “inexperienced, incompetent and incapable of managing the economy or our international reputation”.
But the treasurer said a significant number of Australians see value in the One Nation-aligned message of returning to the “good old days”.
double quotation markOur role as progressive people is not to scold those who see appeal in that message. It’s not to mock them, dare I say cancel them, or talk down to them.
He said the government should instead genuinely acknowledge the pressures people are under and deliver measures to make people’s lives better.

double quotation markThe far right strategy is to divide people and it’s working; their goal is to talk down our economy so that their endless negativity becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Their core message is often clear and sometimes very appealing: let’s just go back to a more nostalgic version of the world we remember. We have all the facts to push back on this, but facts don’t beat feelings. Feelings are as real as facts.
Welcome
Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Vatican confirms Pope Leo underwent surgery for lung cancer
articles.summary: The pope has had part of his lung removed and is recovering after surgery. Leo has been unusually candid for a pontiff about his health issues, disclosing the surgery to thousands of people in St.…

image.caption: Leo was greeted by the hospital's medical director, Andrea Cambieri, before he went in for his procedureImage: Guglielmo Mangiapane/REUTERS

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV underwent surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung that later was reported to be cancerous, the Vatican said, adding the pope "woke up normally" after the procedure.
"The procedure was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned," said a brief Vatican statement.
The Vatican ​said in a medical bulletin that he lower lobe of Leo's right lung was removed, and he was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common ​form of lung cancer.
The Vatican said the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests and was confirmed during surgery.

The surgery at Rome's prestigious Gemelli hospital, which has been the main site of treatment for popes for decades, lasted about 7 hours. Leo's recovery is expected to ​take about a week, the statement added.
According to oncologists, Leo has an excellent prognosis since the cancerous nodule was caught so early.
A Vatican source cited by AFP news agency said further tests were being carried out to determine if the cancer had spread further.
Shift in transparency
Leo, 71, disclosed the health issue to thousands of worshippers at a prayer service on Sunday, making a marked shift in the level of transparency about his health compared to his predecessors.
In the past, the Vatican has often been accused of making confusing or extremely vague statements about popes' health, if revealing at information at all.
All of the pontiff's engagements have been cancelled through October 20. He is still likely to take a planned trip to South America in November.
Pope Leo to undergo lung nodule surgery

articles.title: Tupac Shakur murder trial: Former gang leader Duane Davis sentenced to 40 years
articles.summary: Former Los Angeles gang leader Duane "Keffe D" Davis was found guilty of ordering the killing of hip-hop icon Tupac Shakur

image.caption: Duane Davis, 63, is the only person ever charged in connection with the killing Image: Bizuayehu Tesfaye/Las Vegas Review-Journal/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Duane "Keffe D" Davis was sentenced by a Las Vegas court on Tuesday to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of rap icon Tupac Shakur over 30 years ago.
Shakur was wounded in a drive-by shooting on September 7, 1996, and died in a hospital six days later at the age of 25.
Davis, 63, was convicted in August of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.

"You don't get to take a man from his family. You don't get to take his very life, his whole future from him, and just walk away from it. Especially when that man is Tupac Shakur," Judge Carli Kierny told a Las Vegas court while handing down the sentence.
Shakur was an award-winning rap artist, activist and actor who sold over 75 million records worldwide, many posthumously.
Davis is the only person ever charged in connection with Shakur's killing.

articles.title: ‘Catastrophic’ brake failure, neglected repairs contributed to deadly 2020 icefield bus rollover, judge finds
articles.summary: A complete failure of the braking system triggered by neglected mechanical repairs contributed to a deadly tour bus rollover in the Columbia Icefield, a fatality inquiry has concluded.

image.caption: A rolled-over tour bus rests where it fell on the Columbia Icefield near Jasper, Alta., Sunday, July 19, 2020. A class-action lawsuit alleging the defendants acted recklessly and unreasonably was filed against the operators of a tour bus involved in a fatal rollover at Jasper National Park's Columbi

blocks.text: A complete failure of the braking system triggered by neglected mechanical repairs contributed to a deadly tour bus rollover in the Columbia Icefield, a fatality inquiry has concluded.

In a report made public late last week, Judge Vaughn Myers of the Alberta Court of Justice details a string of catastrophic oversights that preceded the rollover that killed three passengers and severely injured 14.

It was the afternoon of July 18, 2020, when a heavy-duty vehicle known as an Ice Explorer — carrying 24 tourists across the scenic expanse of the Athabasca Glacier in Jasper National Park — tumbled down a steep embankment, landing on its roof.
Dionne Durocher, 24, of North Battleford, Sask., Kamleshbhai Patel, 58, and Griva Patel, 28, of Edmonton, were ejected from the vehicle and died of their injuries within minutes.

In his findings, Myers calls on the tour company Pursuit — also known as Brewster — to make a series of safety improvements, concluding that warnings about the faltering safety of the vehicle went unheeded in the days and weeks before the crash.
The investigation determined the Ice Explorer had dangerously worn components, inadequate brake power and lacked routine maintenance.
Rapid speed, no braking force

Myers said the fatality inquiry, held in October 2025, sought to examine not only policy measures that could prevent similar tragedies but also “questions that were not clearly answered” by the RCMP and Occupational Health and Safety investigators, most critically any lapses in the maintenance of the vehicle.
Ice Explorers are large, wide-bodied, three-axle, off-road buses, also known as snow coaches, that have been used in the Columbia Icefield since the 1980s.

items: Icefield rollover survivor who lost wife wants report released

blocks.text: They’re purpose-built for icy terrain, with specialized brake systems that include a transmission lock-up to assist when the machine is on a descent — but only if the vehicle is in gear.
Court heard that, in the moments before the crash, the Ice Explorer was descending a steep slope known as the Lateral Moraine Road.
The vehicle was in neutral and, lacking engine-retarding force, accelerated to a speed between 41 to 49 km/h, far beyond its maximum powered speed of 14 km/h.
The driver applied the manual brakes, but due to severe mechanical defects, they failed.

items: Partner of Sask. woman who died in Alta. icefield crash calls for increased bus safety

blocks.text: The driver lost control and the bus rolled one and a half times down the slope, with passengers ejected into the rocky terrain below.

“There are two primary contributing factors,” Myers wrote. “The first is the driver, for reasons unknown, negotiating the lateral moraine in neutral and without the six-wheel drive engaged,” Myers wrote.

“This configuration, on such a grade, would create a situation in which vehicle speed accumulates rapidly. Unable to use engine power to slow the bus, the driver would have to rely on conventional braking.”
Pursuit’s policy at the time was for drivers to put the Ice Explorers in neutral at the top of the hill and then, at the start of the steepest descent, put them in gear.
In this case, the bus was never put into gear or it popped out of gear almost immediately, the judge found.

“This leads to the second primary contributing factor: effective braking force. During the mechanical inspection, it was determined that this vehicle did not have sufficient braking power to stop the vehicle, even in ideal situations.”
'Worn, improperly inspected'
An inspection after the crash showed that only one of the six wheels had the power to safely brake as required.

Court heard that five days before the crash, a driver formally reported a major braking issue on a daily inspection report. He noted that full pedal depression was required to stop the rig and requested an inspection of the brake slack adjusters.
But the defect wasn’t inspected or repaired, nor was it carried forward on subsequent daily reports as the company required, the judge found.

items: Witness surprised anyone survived bus crash in Jasper National Park that killed 3, injured 24

blocks.text: Furthermore, on-site mechanics were new and inexperienced with Ice Explorers and also lacked proper training, the inquiry found.
“In short, the brakes suffered a catastrophic failure because they were worn, improperly inspected and concerns with respect to the brakes functioning were not attended to,” Myers wrote.
'Inconceivable to the court'
Court also heard the Ice Explorer bus had been serviced two months earlier by Wajax, a company that offers repairs and maintenance for heavy-duty vehicles.
It was sent to Wajax for a scheduled 1,000-hour inspection, returning to service just 12 days before the fatal crash.
However, the judge noted serious issues with the Wajax inspection report, which was undated and did not reference a specific vehicle.
“The inspection report tendered indicated the brakes were satisfactory and passed inspection,” Myers wrote.

“It is inconceivable to the court that the tires were removed to properly inspect the faulty braking. Secondly, the court has serious concerns whether this inspection report actually applied to this vehicle.”

items: Icefield buses add seatbelts, resume tours nearly 1 year after Jasper, Alta., crash

blocks.text: Myers said the lack of seatbelts and the route itself were contributing factors. Parts of Lateral Moraine Road reach an incline of 40 per cent, exceeding the maximum limit of 36 per cent specified by the Ice Explorer manufacturer.
The court determined that though medical response was prompt, no intervention could have saved the victims.
Myers called on Pursuit to improve its inspection protocols.
The company must ensure that external maintenance and inspection reports are dated and detail exactly what work is performed on which vehicle, and that a copy is kept inside for driver review.
The company should also work alongside OHS and the provincial government to immediately implement a training program for all mechanics working on its Ice Explorer fleet, Myers wrote.
The judge encouraged OHS and Alberta Transportation to establish a rigorous, standardized three-year service and inspection procedure for off-road tour vehicles and a new policy for defect reports.

items: Court date set in advance of fatality inquiry into deadly Columbia Icefield bus rollover

blocks.text: RCMP didn't lay criminal charges in the crash, but Pursuit pleaded guilty in 2023 to two charges under the Alberta Occupational Health and Safety Act and was fined $475,000.

In a statement to CBC News, officials with Pursuit said the operator has since made significant safety changes including enhanced driver training, seatbelts in all Ice Explorers, and updated processes for vehicle inspection, maintenance and defect reports.

items: 'It's not easy': Survivors of deadly Icefield tour bus crash near Jasper, Alta., file $17M lawsuit

blocks.text: “[We] will continue working with the appropriate authorities to ensure our practices meet the standard expected of us.
“Our thoughts remain with the families of Dionne Durocher, Griva Patel and Kamleshbhai Patel and with everyone affected by the July 2020 tragedy at the Columbia Icefield.”

articles.title: Trump ousts Kimberly Guilfoyle as US ambassador to Greece after corruption allegations
articles.summary: Guilfoyle the allegations of improper conduct are "false" and being ambassador was the "honour of a lifetime".

blocks.text: President Donald Trump's administration has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign from her position as US ambassador to Greece, White House press secretary Katie Zacharia has announced.

Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host, had been facing mounting scrutiny after reports she allegedly asked a Trump donor to pay her hefty credit card bill in exchange for access to his administration and behaving inappropriately while in Athens.
Trump said she had done a good job, but she will "not be there" in Greece any longer. "I didn't like what I read," he said.
Guilfoyle vowed to defend herself against the "false" claims and said the ambassadorship had been the "honour of a lifetime".
Zacharia announced during her first - and unusually short - media briefing that Guilfoyle "had been asked to resign" without providing more details.
"She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well," she said.
Guilfoyle, the 57-year-old ex-wife of California Governor Gavin Newsom, was first nominated as envoy to Athens in December 2024, a month before Trump returned to the White House as president.
In a lengthy post on X, Guilfoyle thanked President Trump, said she would always be a loyal supporter and denied any wrongdoing.
"I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity," she wrote, adding that she will "not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service".
Her position had become increasingly tenuous as allegations of improper behaviour mounted over the past week.
A series of text messages seen by the BBC - and first reported by The Wall Street Journal - appear to show Guilfoyle asking for the money from Eric Deters, a long-time Trump ally.
"It won't show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express," she wrote in one Signal message.
In another message - dated just days before her US Senate confirmation hearing last July - Guilfoyle wrote: "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today."
Guilfoyle's lawyers disputed the authenticity of the messages and said she was asking for money owed to her for speeches and consulting work conducted on his behalf before she became ambassador.

Audio recordings obtained by the Wall Street Journal reportedly include Guilfoyle bragging about her connections to prominent Greek business tycoons who she said bankrolled luxury travel and flights on private jets.
According to the newspaper, she also boasted to an official in Athens that the US could topple the Greek government.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was pictured alongside Guilfoyle during a trip to Athens last week, also had reportedly become unhappy with the allegations.
Following the news that Guilfoyle was being asked to leave, Deters told the BBC that "it's a great day for American diplomacy".

Deters, who said he did not ultimately pay Guilfoyle, also said it was a "complete lie" that he owed her money for speaking and consulting fees and said he is planning to take legal action against her.
Guilfoyle was a longtime political ally of Trump's and was for years in a relationship with his son Donald Jr, to whom she got engaged in 2018.
That relationship ended in 2024, around the time she was appointed to the position in Greece.

Trump noted on Tuesday that "she, I guess, dated my son a long time ago" but was not like a family member. The US president said he did not speak with Guilfoyle before she was asked to resign. "She went to Greece, she was doing a good job, but we didn't like what we were reading," Trump said.
The president also said he thought Zacharia was "very good" in her first White House press briefing.
Zacharia, a longtime conservative commentator and Trump supporter, only answered a handful of questions during the 14-minute briefing.

For the first eight minutes, she read a list of what the administration sees as policy achievements. Then Zacharia answered questions about Guilfoyle, Ukraine, her family and administration policies towards non-traditional media outlets.
She said she viewed her job as working to "amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump's incredible agenda".

articles.title: Germany news: Left-leaning Berlin coalition talks break down
articles.summary: The SPD and Greens in Berlin have halted exploratory coalition talks with the Left Party amid a dispute over Israel policy and antisemitism. DW has more.

image.caption: Less than a week ago the three parties agreed to enter exploratory coalition talks, but already they're on the ropes [FILE: October 8, 2026]Image: Annette Riedl/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: October 13, 2026
Why have the Berlin exploratory talks broken down within a week?

The breakdown in the exploratory talks can be traced back to concerns about the often highly critical stance on Israel adopted by some members of the Left Party, coupled with criticism of the appearance of a figure linked to organized crime at an election night party.

The Left scored well with parts of Berlin's population, not least the young and communities with more people of migrant backgrounds, with an unusually stern line on Israeli wars in Gaza and elsewhere in the Middle East by the often muted standards of German politics.

But comments from its more outspoken members and controversies like an organized crime boss attending an election-night after-party led to questions — particularly in some newspapers and from the conservative Christian Democrats — about whether center-left parties could work under the Left's leadership.
In a bid to settle this, the Greens, SPD and Left drafted a joint statement on antisemitism, Israel's right to exist and maintaining a distance from organized crime before starting their talks.
But the text subsequently faced criticism from within the Left's own ranks.
On Tuesday, as 44 Left Party members of the new Berlin parliament met, they instead signed off on a different text more closely aligned to the party's past internal position papers.

"We stand by Israel's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Israel. Equally we stand by Palestine's right to exist and for equal rights for all people in Palestine," the Left Party's text read.

Among other things, this omits a reference in the joint text to Israel's right to exist being "non-negotiable," and to listing potential sanctions for transgressions potentially extending as far as being ejected from the party.
The CDU — which emerged as the second-largest party in the vote, well adrift of the Left on 18.8% — argue that the SPD and Greens should negotiate a coalition government with them instead.

Chancellor Merz had also weighed into the discussion, saying that the allegations of impropriety facing the Left Party cannot be "dismissed with a piece of paper." In the meantime, the party's state lawmakers appear to have disavowed that piece of paper anyway.
What's behind the rising polarization in German politics?

articles.title: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby defends family's enrolment in $10-a-day child-care
articles.summary: NDP Leader David Eby is defending his family's enrolment in British Columbia's $10-a-day child-care program. Eby is under attack from Conservatives who say his "wealthy family" should not benefit…

image.caption: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is fending off attacks from the B.C. Conservatives about his family's use of the provincial $10-a-day child-care program. (Nav Rahi/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

NDP Leader David Eby is defending his family's enrolment in British Columbia's $10-a-day child-care program. Eby is under attack from Conservatives who say his "wealthy family" should not benefit from the program that they say is inaccessible to many low-income families.
Eby's family has accessed subsidized child-care program which Conservative opponents say is 'shocking'
B.C. NDP Leader David Eby is defending his family's enrolment in the provincial $10-a-day child-care program.
Eby is under attack from Conservatives who say his "wealthy family" should not benefit from the program that they say is inaccessible to many low-income families.
In a post on X Monday, Eby said one of his children was already attending a child-care centre when it was designated as a $10-a-day site.
"When that occurred, we chose as a family to make a donation to that excellent facility," Eby said.
"We felt that we did not need that discount and we wanted to make sure that the child-care centre could provide other supports for families in the community."
Eby said his family will make a similar donation to the child-care centre for their youngest child who attends the same facility.
At a news conference on Tuesday, Eby would not specify the donation amount or if it was used as a tax write off.
"We certainly didn't need that discount," Eby said.
"We paid the difference between what it was before and what it was after the $10-a-day daycare," he added.

items: More stories from Vancouver Island

blocks.text: Now, Eby is taking heat from the B.C. Conservatives during the snap provincial election campaign.

"It's shocking to learn that while hundreds of thousands of British Columbians are struggling with the most expensive child care in the country, David Eby's family landed a plum $10-a-day child care spot," said Margareta Dovgal, the B.C. Conservative candidate for Vancouver-Yaletown, in a news release Monday.

The Conservatives called attention to Eby's compensation from 2025 to 2026 as premier, which totalled more than $226,000, and criticized his "wealthy family" for benefiting from the subsidized child-care program.
After Eby's Tuesday news conference, Dovgal said Eby was dodging the tough questions.

"David Eby should look a working single mother paying thousands in childcare costs in the eye explaining why his wealthy, powerful family deserves $10/day childcare first," Dovgal said in a second news release.
"David Eby is trying to defend the indefensible, as British Columbians are seeing Eby for the opportunistic hypocrite he is."

The Conservatives are demanding Eby answer a number of questions, including around the value and proof of his first donation, whether it was a tax write-off, and more information on the value of the second planned donation.
What is the $10-a-day child-care program?

The $10-a-day program is operated by independent businesses who have chosen to participate; access to one of the facilities is based on each location's licensed capacity and waitlist, according to the provincial government.
When a child-care centre is approved to be a part of the $10-a-day program, the child's space is automatically converted into the $10-a-day program, according to a provincial Q&A webpage.

According to the webpage, which was last updated in 2024, there were more than 13,200 $10-a-day child-care spaces throughout B.C. The Ministry of Education and Child Care would not provide an updated number of spaces as the government is in a temporary caretaker mode due to the election.
The B.C. NDP say their Conservative opponents "have been silent" around whether their party would reverse child care fee caps.
Eby said Tuesday the Conservatives are proposing to cut certain child-care programs. However, the Conservatives have not laid out their plan yet.
CBC News has reached out to the B.C. Conservatives for their child-care proposals.

articles.title: Saudi coalition strikes fuel depot near Yemen's capital
articles.summary: The Houthis have warned Saudi Arabia that they will retaliate by targeting the Saudi cities of Riyadh and Dammam.

blocks.text: The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen has carried out a strike on fuel depot near the Houthi-controlled capital, Sanaa, its spokesperson says.
Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of using the Yemen Petroleum Company's al-Sabaha facility to fuel their war effort, including by supporting missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia.
The coalition earlier warned civilians to evacuate the site ahead of a "special operation", with Houthi media saying the facility had been struck before al-Maliki confirmed the strike.
The Houthis have warned they will retaliate by targeting the airport and Aramco refinery in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, and Aramco's headquarters in the eastern city of Dammam.
It came as the Saudi cabinet, chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, said the Iran-backed group would "bear the consequences" of its recent deadly attacks on the kingdom.
Thirteen people were killed when a missile hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday, while another person was killed in a similar attack there the following day.
On Tuesday, the coalition said its forces had destroyed three drones north of Riyadh.

The Houthis have said they are targeting airports, oil and gas facilities, and military bases in Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones in response to deadly Saudi strikes on territory that they control in western Yemen, including Sanaa.
The Saudi-led coalition has been providing air support for Yemeni pro-government forces mounting an offensive on Yemen's Red Sea coast and several other front lines.

A correspondent for AFP news agency reported that queues formed at petrol stations in Sanaa on Tuesday afternoon following the coalition's warning of an impending operation against the al-Sabaha oil facility, with many residents worried about shortages.
The Yemen Petroleum Company, which is run by the Houthis, issued a statement that sought to reassure them, saying the facility "does not contain any stock of petroleum products".

The company also said it had "taken all necessary precautionary measures to address any emergency, ensuring the stability of the supply situation and the continued meeting of citizens' needs in a normal manner".

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

The conflict escalated in September after the Houthis seized part of Yemen's south-western Red Sea coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for global shipping. Their advance contributed to a rise in oil prices following six months of war between the US, Israel and Iran.
Last week, pro-government forces said they had regained control of territory overlooking Bab al-Mandab after launching a major counter-offensive with the support of Saudi air strikes.
Hundreds of people have reportedly been killed in Yemen since August. The UN's human rights office says they include at least 54 civilians, half of them children.
More than 216,000 people have also been displaced across the country, and suspected cholera cases have tripled in three weeks, rising from 217 to 647, according to the UN.

articles.title: Ex-gang boss sentenced to 40 years for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder
articles.summary: The sentence marks an end to the mystery around Tupac's cold case, which has intrigued hip-hop fans for nearly 30 years.

blocks.text: The key evidence in the case were Davis' own words, in which he repeatedly and publicly acknowledged being inside the white Cadillac from where the deadly shots were fired.

In exchange for being shielded from criminal prosecution, he had told authorities about his role in Shakur's death during a secret 2008 police interview related to the death of fellow rapper Notorious B.I.G., real name Christopher Wallace, who was killed in a shooting just months after Shakur.
Davis elaborated further on his role in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend, which led to publicity and media interviews.

But the book and interviews he offered elaborating on his role in Shakur's killing voided a protective agreement he had established with authorities that had blocked any criminal charges from being filed. A judge then allowed his police interview to be used in the murder trial against him.
Shakur was 25 years old and at the height of his career as one of rap's most influential voices at the time of his death. He has sold more than 75 million records worldwide.
For three decades, the investigation into his killing remained one of America's most famous cold cases, spurring countless conspiracies - until the conviction of Davis last month.
Throughout the trial, Davis' defence team tried to persuade jurors that his comments were fiction - bravado and exaggeration intended to sell books and make money.

Prosecutors argued that although Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips street gang, did not himself fire the gun, he ordered the shooting and supplied the gun that his nephew Orlando Anderson used to open fire.
Anderson died in an unrelated shooting in 1998, having denied involvement in the killing of Shakur.

articles.title: Ukraine allies in Poland after Starlink sabotage, Trump diesel deal
articles.summary: Germany's Johann Wadephul said hybrid plots like the Starlink fire showed Europe was "in Russia's crosshairs." The UK's Ed Miliband said Trump's Russian diesel deal led to a "very difficult few days"…

image.caption: German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said sanctions should continue being imposed on Russia's economy as attacks on Ukraine persistImage: Jörg Blank/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The foreign ministers of Germany, Norway, Poland and the UK spoke at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday.

This came as investigators in Germany were chasing down suspects for a fire at a Starlink station in Poland, and as Ukraine's European allies scrambled to deal with US President Donald Trump's latest lurch into Vladimir Putin's lap.
What did the ministers say about Russian diesel and Ukraine?

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul bemoaned the US decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as part of a deal to supply the US — seemingly struck as Trump panics about fuel prices with the Iran war still unresolved and a month to go until midterm elections.
"I would say this is not the time to lower the sanctions regime but to strengthen this," Wadephul said, noting the new package of EU sanctions imposed on Monday.
